1: //! # pathland-core-transport
2: //!
3: //! How Pathland opcodes are transported from the guest engine to host
4: //! renderers. There are two peer backends:
5: //!
6: //! - **Shared memory** (desktop/native/WASM): the ring buffer + arena in
7: //!   `pathland-core` (`Guest`/`Host`). Zero-copy. This crate treats it as
8: //!   the local transport — no duplication.
9: //! - **Network batch** (SSR → browser): opcodes + string data serialized into
10: //!   **batches**.
11: //!
12: //! There are two network codecs, for two different relationships between the
13: //! producer and the consumer:
14: //!
15: //! - **Self-contained frames** ([`encode_frame`] / [`decode_frame`]) — each
16: //!   batch carries its own string section and `SET_TEXT` references strings by
17: //!   a *relative* offset into that section. The consumer needs **no prior
18: //!   state**: every message is independent. This is the streaming codec used
19: //!   for live deltas over WebSocket.
20: //! - **Arena-delta batches** ([`encode_batch`] / [`BatchEncoder`] /
21: //!   [`BatchDecoder`]) — the batch carries only the bytes *appended* to the
22: //!   arena since the previous batch, and `SET_TEXT` references absolute arena
23: //!   offsets. The consumer mirrors the arena so those offsets stay valid. This
24: //!   mirrors the shared-memory arena over a wire and is the ring-compatible
25: //!   codec (kept for a future WASM/embedded guest).
26: //!
27: //! ## Batch wire format (both codecs share the header)
28: //!
29: //! ```text
30: //! magic "PLPL" (u32 LE) | version (u16) | flags (u16) | frameCount (u32)
31: //! | opcodeCount (u32) | opcodes (16 B × opcodeCount) | stringsLen (u32)
32: //! | string bytes (length-prefixed entries: [u32 len][bytes])
33: //! ```
34: //!
35: //! For a self-contained frame the trailing section is that frame's own string
36: //! table; for an arena-delta batch it is the arena bytes appended since the
37: //! last batch.
38: //!
39: //! ## Example (producer)
40: //!
41: //! ```no_run
42: //! use pathland_core_transport::{Batcher, BatchPolicy, BatchEncoder};
43: //! use std::time::Duration;
44: //!
45: //! let policy = BatchPolicy::new(Duration::from_millis(4), 1400);
46: //! let mut batcher = Batcher::new(policy);
47: //! let mut encoder = BatchEncoder::new();
48: //!
49: //! // batcher.push_frame(&frame) accumulates opcodes + arena delta;
50: //! // batcher.flush() -> Option<Vec<u8>> produces the serialized batch.
51: //! ```
52:

687: ### Sequence gap detection
688: 
689: The network backend is reliable and ordered **within a connection**, but a
690: middlebox can drop a batch while the socket stays "open", and a producer's send
691: path can wedge — either way the consumer silently misses deltas. The batch
692: `sequence` makes that loss detectable:
693: 
694: - **Producer**: maintain one monotonic `sequence` per stream, incremented by
695:   exactly one for **each encoded batch**. Only guest → host delta batches
696:   consume a sequence number; heartbeat (`META::PING`/`PONG`) and request
697:   batches (`META::RESYNC`, `META::ENVIRONMENT`, events) carry `0` and never
698:   advance it.
699: - **Consumer**: the first guest → host batch establishes a baseline
700:   (`expected = sequence + 1`). Every later guest → host batch MUST satisfy
701:   `sequence == expected`; then `expected = sequence + 1`. A batch whose
702:   sequence does not match means one or more batches were lost.
703: - **Recovery**: on a gap the consumer MUST NOT apply the gapped batch (its
704:   deltas assume the lost state) and MUST request a full snapshot
705:   (`META::RESYNC`), then re-baseline on the next guest → host batch. The
706:   consumer also re-baselines on every (re)connect.
707: - **Heartbeat batches are exempt**: a `META::PONG` (host → guest) is not part of
708:   the guest → host stream; consumers track only guest → host batches.
709: 
710: The recovery is **always a full snapshot**, never retransmission: the renderer
711: is stateless and the application owns the retained tree, so a `META::RESYNC`
712: reconverges the consumer regardless of what was lost. **Acknowledgements and a
713: retransmit queue are deliberately not part of the protocol** — they would add a
714: per-session send buffer and an ack exchange to a design whose recovery is
715: already a stateless snapshot.
716: 
717: ### Transport heartbeat
718: 
719: The **network batch backend** (a WebSocket / streamed connection) can fail
720: silently: a proxy or load balancer may drop the connection without a close
721: frame, or the peer's send path may wedge, leaving the socket "open" while
722: nothing is delivered. Neither side can detect this from the batch stream alone.

## Current state

The Java server routes **inbound** event batches only: `PathlandSession` (route an inbound event batch into the app's bindings) and `PathlandRegistry` (`MAX_EVENT_BATCH`, per-session routing). Outbound frames are sent **one WS message per frame** — there is no time/size coalescing.

<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<project xmlns="http://maven.apache.org/POM/4.0.0"
         xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance"
         xsi:schemaLocation="http://maven.apache.org/POM/4.0.0 http://maven.apache.org/xsd/maven-4.0.0.xsd">
    <modelVersion>4.0.0</modelVersion>

    <parent>
        <groupId>org.pathland</groupId>
        <artifactId>pathland-parent</artifactId>
        <version>0.1.0</version>
    </parent>

    <artifactId>pathland-observability</artifactId>
    <packaging>jar</packaging>

    <name>Pathland Observability</name>
    <description>
        Observability adapters for the framework-agnostic Pathland server runtime: a
        Micrometer PathlandTelemetry (pathland.* counters/timers + a sessions gauge) and an
        opt-in OpenTelemetry TracingTelemetry decorator (spans per frame send / event
        batch / SSR render). The starters auto-wire these when a MeterRegistry/Tracer bean
        is present; without them the core stays on PathlandTelemetry.NOOP.
    </description>

    <dependencies>
        <dependency>
            <groupId>org.pathland</groupId>
            <artifactId>pathland-server-core</artifactId>
            <version>${project.version}</version>
        </dependency>
        <dependency>
            <groupId>io.micrometer</groupId>
            <artifactId>micrometer-core</artifactId>
        </dependency>
        <!-- The OTel API is optional: only needed when the host enables tracing. The
             starters add the OTel bridge/exporters that bring it in. -->
        <dependency>
            <groupId>io.opentelemetry</groupId>
            <artifactId>opentelemetry-api</artifactId>
            <optional>true</optional>
        </dependency>
        <dependency>
            <groupId>org.junit.jupiter</groupId>
            <artifactId>junit-jupiter</artifactId>
            <scope>test</scope>
        </dependency>
        <dependency>
            <groupId>io.micrometer</groupId>
            <artifactId>micrometer-core</artifactId>
            <scope>test</scope>
        </dependency>
    </dependencies>
</project>

Then, at runtime, if a `Tracer` bean exists (because the app added `quarkus-opentelemetry`), wrap; else no-op. Quarkus provides a `Tracer` bean only if `quarkus-opentelemetry` is present. For Spring: `micrometer-tracing-bridge-otel` + `opentelemetry-exporter-otlp` provide an `io.opentelemetry.api.trace.Tracer`? - Spring: `ObjectProvider<io.opentelemetry.api.trace.Tracer>`.

...

# pathland-observability — implementation status

**Last updated:** October 3, 2026

Observability adapters for the framework-agnostic `pathland-server-core`
telemetry seam. The core emits lifecycle/throughput events through
`PathlandTelemetry` (default `NOOP`); this module turns them into metrics and
spans. Protocol/contract context: `spec/OPCODE.md`; the seam itself is in
`pathland-server-core`.

## Implemented

- **`MicrometerTelemetry`** — a `PathlandTelemetry` over any Micrometer
  `MeterRegistry` (Prometheus, OTLP, …). Metric catalog:
  - `pathland.sessions.active` — gauge (pull-based, bound by the host)
  - `pathland.sessions.opened` / `pathland.sessions.closed` — counters
  - `pathland.events.received` — counter (decoded inbound events)
  - `pathland.batches.sent` / `pathland.frames.sent` / `pathland.bytes.sent` — counters
  - `pathland.batch.size` — distribution summary (opcodes per batch)
  - `pathland.batch.flush` — timer (merge + encode)
  - `pathland.ssr.render` — timer (SSR render round-trip)
  - `pathland.resync.requested` — counter
  - `pathland.ws.failures` — counter
  - Every meter is tagged by `mount` (bounded). Registrations are idempotent, so
    a builder per event is cheap and cannot leak meters.
- **`TracingTelemetry`** — an OpenTelemetry decorator over another
  `PathlandTelemetry`: emits a span per frame send (`pathland.frame.send`), per
  inbound event batch (`pathland.event.batch`), and per SSR render
  (`pathland.ssr.render`), with the wrapped telemetry still receiving every
  event. Spans are back-dated by the measured duration so they render with the
  real latency. Opt-in — the starters build it only when a `Tracer`/`OpenTelemetry`
  bean is available.

## Not implemented / gaps

- No client-side (browser) telemetry — server-side only.
- `ws.failures` does not tag the failure reason (unbounded cardinality).

## Verified by

`mvn test -pl pathland-observability` — `MicrometerTelemetryTest` (the full
metric catalog + per-mount tagging) and `TracingTelemetryTest` (span names via an
in-memory OTel exporter, plus delegation). The starters' tests assert the wiring
end to end (`/q/health` + `/q/metrics`, `/actuator/health` + `pathland.*` meters).

1: # pathland-quarkus-starter — implementation status
2: 
3: **Last updated:** September 27, 2026
4: 
5: Quarkus integration for Pathland: SSR at any path, live deltas over each app's reserved
6: `/{base}/ws`, per-session state. Adding the starter dependency + a `PathlandApp` CDI
7: bean gives a running app; `MountedApp` beans host more apps at their own subpaths
8: (the BFF layout).
9: 
10: ## Implemented
11: 
12: - **`PathlandSocket`** — `@WebSocket("/_pathland/ws")` for the root app: 1:1 sessions
13:   per connection (a fresh `uiId` per connection + the client's `wid` state scope from
14:   the `?wid=` query param), binary events routed into the root registry of the
15:   `PathlandHost`. **Stateless (critical)**: quarkus-websockets-next endpoints default
16:   to `@Singleton` — one shared instance for all connections — so the per-connection
17:   ids come from `connection.id()` + the handshake and the `QuarkusConnection` adapters
18:   live in a map keyed by connection id. Memoizing `uiId`/`wid`/`transport` on the
19:   shared instance collapsed every connection onto ONE session (multiple browsers shared
20:   one UI model — a probe or second tab drove the first tab's session).
21: - **`MountedPathlandSocket`** — `@WebSocket("/{app}/_pathland/ws")` for mounted apps:
22:   the `{app}` path param resolves the app's registry. Mount paths are single-segment.
23:   Same stateless rule as the root socket.
24: - **`IndexResource`** — JAX-RS SSR catch-all (`/` + deep links, `/_pathland/**` excluded
25:   via negative lookahead) dispatching to the longest-mount app (prefix stripped);
26:   SSR renders defaults (no session cookie — per-window state arrives over the WS);
27:   per-app framework files (`/{app}/_pathland/...`, e.g. the mounted app's bundle) are
28:   served from the shared `/_pathland/**` classpath mount. Quarkus serves the global
29:   `/_pathland/**` bundle + asset mount from `META-INF/resources` before JAX-RS.
30: - **`PathlandRegistryProducer`** — CDI `@Produces @Singleton` `PathlandHost` from every
31:   `MountedApp` bean plus the lone `PathlandApp` bean (mounted at `/`); `@Disposes` shuts
32:   it down. Reads the `pathland.debug-html` config property (default `false`) to enable
33:   per-node HTML comments in SSR output.
34: - **`QuarkusConnection`** — adapts `WebSocketConnection` to `PathlandConnection`.
35:   Sends are **serialized** (one `sendBinary` subscription in flight, the rest queued),
36:   and a **send failure closes the connection** so the session drops it and the DOM
37:   client reconnects + `META::RESYNC` (recoverable) instead of silently stalling on an
38:   "open" socket that never delivers (the remote seekbar symptom). **Send timeout**: a
39:   `sendBinary` that neither completes nor fails within 10 s (a half-dead connection /
40:   a dropped proxy upstream leg) is marked failed and closed — a hung send would
41:   otherwise wedge the serialized drain forever. **Keep-alive pings**: the connection
42:   sends a WS-protocol ping every 15 s (browsers auto-pong) to keep the connection warm
43:   through middleboxes and detect a dead client; `close()` stops the keep-alive
44:   scheduler (the sockets' `@OnClose` calls it).
45: - **Heartbeat** — both sockets reply to a client `META::PING` with a `META::PONG`
46:   **at the transport layer** (through their `QuarkusConnection`, no actor/session
47:   dependency, and a PING never creates or wakes a session); spec/OPCODE.md
48:   §Transport heartbeat.
49: - **Failure handling** — `fail()` logs the reason; `close()` (socket `@OnClose`)
50:   no longer calls `close()` on the already-closed connection (no spurious
51:   "Connection already closed" noise). A **transient write failure on a connection
52:   that still reports open is logged, not closed** — only a confirmed-dead channel
53:   (or a send hung past the timeout) warrants closing. The send-timeout task is
54:   **cancelled when the send completes**, so a completed-but-late callback can't
55:   false-time-out and kill a healthy connection. Keep-alive pings are sent directly
56:   (Vert.x serializes writes — no sync with `sendBinary` needed).
57: - `META-INF/beans.xml` so Quarkus discovers the starter.
58:

60:

63: public class MyApp {
64:     @Produces @Singleton PathlandApp main() { return () -> new MyHomeView(); }
65:     @Produces @Singleton MountedApp support() { return MountedApp.of("/support", ...); }
66: }

76: probe) and asserts each connects, re-syncs, gets transport-level PONGs, stays isolated,
77: and is never closed by the peer.

## Summary

On unstable connections, important messages can be lost **silently** and never be received:

- **Server → client deltas**: on a half-open/silently-broken connection (NAT/keepalive drop, proxy frame loss, dead peer) the server keeps sending into a socket that "looks" open; no close is detected, so the existing reconnect + `META::RESYNC` recovery never fires → stale UI.
- **Client → server events**: browser `send()` is optimistic, so an important `VALUE_CHANGED`/`TEXT_CHANGED` sent into a broken connection is dropped and **neither side notices** → stale app state.

TCP already guarantees ordering/no-loss on a genuinely live connection, and detected drops already recover via reconnect + `META::RESYNC`. The gap is **undetectable** loss (half-open) and **client→server event** loss. The fix is a lightweight, sequence-based **built-in ACK** that makes delivery observable and drives the existing recovery paths.

## Design

**Protocol (spec-first):**
- New `META::ACK = 0x04` (both directions; `spec/OPCODE.md` + `pathland-core` constant + `Commands.Meta.ACK` + a `spec/CONFORMANCE.md` golden vector). Field `A` = the highest contiguous sequence counter of the **peer's** stream this side processed.
  - client→server: ACKs server frame batches (recovery + liveness).
  - server→client: ACKs the client's event sequence (lets the client drop its retransmit buffer; doubles as the heartbeat).
- Sequencing contract (network-batch section): every server→client batch carries a per-session monotonic `frameCount` (field exists today — Java server sends 0); every client→server event batch carries a per-connection monotonic event sequence.

**Server (`pathland-server-core`):**
- Stamp each flushed batch with an incrementing `frameCount`.
- **Bounded replay buffer** (~last 64 frames / ~256 KB) of sent batches; evicted as the client ACKs. On an ACK **gap** → replay `ack+1..lastSent` in order; beyond the buffer → server-driven `META::RESYNC` fallback.
- **Liveness**: per-session `lastClientActivity`; no ACK/message within ~30 s → drop the connection (client reconnects + RESYNC). Keep the existing Quarkus send-failure-close.
- **Event ACK**: track the last processed client event sequence; emit `META::ACK` (server→client) in the next batch + a periodic idle heartbeat.

**Client (`lib/typescript`):**
- Track the highest **contiguous applied** `frameCount`; send throttled `META::ACK` (~250 ms) + idle heartbeat.
- Stamp outbound event batches with an event sequence; **buffer unacked events** (latest-per-control, bounded); drop acked on the server ACK; **resend unacked on reconnect** (events are idempotent).
- **Read-timeout liveness**: no server message within ~15–30 s → close → reconnect + RESYNC (catches a dead server client-side too).

## Notes
- No per-message retransmission of server deltas beyond the bounded replay buffer; reconnect+RESYNC stays the ultimate recovery.
- Replayed frames are safe: TCP ordering means the client never applies anything beyond its ack, so replay delivers exactly the missing frames; reconnect is deduped by RESYNC.
- `status.md` updates for `pathland-core`, `pathland-server-core`, `lib/typescript`.

## Verification
Rust conformance vector; Java tests (batcher sequencing, replay-on-gap, buffer-overflow→RESYNC, ack-timeout close, server→client ACK); TS tests (applied-frameCount tracking, throttled ACK, reconnect resends unacked events, read-timeout); live flaky-link check against the Quarkus demo.

Related: #114 (Quarkus send-failure-close), #115 (delta batching).

687: ### Sequence gap detection
688: 
689: The network backend is reliable and ordered **within a connection**, but a
690: middlebox can drop a batch while the socket stays "open", and a producer's send
691: path can wedge — either way the consumer silently misses deltas. The batch
692: `sequence` makes that loss detectable:
693: 
694: - **Producer**: maintain one monotonic `sequence` per stream, incremented by
695:   exactly one for **each encoded batch**. Only guest → host delta batches
696:   consume a sequence number; heartbeat (`META::PING`/`PONG`) and request
697:   batches (`META::RESYNC`, `META::ENVIRONMENT`, events) carry `0` and never
698:   advance it.
699: - **Consumer**: the first guest → host batch establishes a baseline
700:   (`expected = sequence + 1`). Every later guest → host batch MUST satisfy
701:   `sequence == expected`; then `expected = sequence + 1`. A batch whose
702:   sequence does not match means one or more batches were lost.
703: - **Recovery**: on a gap the consumer MUST NOT apply the gapped batch (its
704:   deltas assume the lost state) and MUST request a full snapshot
705:   (`META::RESYNC`), then re-baseline on the next guest → host batch. The
706:   consumer also re-baselines on every (re)connect.
707: - **Heartbeat batches are exempt**: a `META::PONG` (host → guest) is not part of
708:   the guest → host stream; consumers track only guest → host batches.
709: 
710: The recovery is **always a full snapshot**, never retransmission: the renderer
711: is stateless and the application owns the retained tree, so a `META::RESYNC`
712: reconverges the consumer regardless of what was lost. **Acknowledgements and a
713: retransmit queue are deliberately not part of the protocol** — they would add a
714: per-session send buffer and an ack exchange to a design whose recovery is
715: already a stateless snapshot.

719: The **network batch backend** (a WebSocket / streamed connection) can fail
720: silently: a proxy or load balancer may drop the connection without a close
721: frame, or the peer's send path may wedge, leaving the socket "open" while

So:
- Client sends PING, server replies PONG (transport layer).
- Server keep-alive: QuarkusConnection sends WS-protocol-level ping every 15s.
- No server-side `lastClientActivity` / idle-drop based on absence of PING. But the WS-protocol pings (auto-answered) + send-failure-close handle host-side detection.
- No ACK.

So #117's design (ACK + replay buffer + event retransmit) is **not implemented and is now explicitly rejected by the spec**.

Now, the question "Is #117 still relevant?" I should answer with a clear assessment:

**Partially.** The *problem* framing still has one real unaddressed piece (client→server event loss on a half-open connection), but the *proposed solution* (built-in ACK, frame sequencing for server→client, replay buffer, event retransmit) is now largely obsolete/superseded and partly contradicts the current spec:

1. **Server→client sequencing**: #117 proposed `frameCount` (field A). #58 already implemented this as `sequence` (field at offset 8), with gap detection + RESYNC. So that sub-item is DONE (differently named).
2. **Liveness/heartbeat**: #117's `lastClientActivity` + 30s drop and "read-timeout liveness". The heartbeat work (#119/#120) implemented client PING/server PONG + client watchdog + server keep-alive + send-timeout-close. So the liveness half is DONE (by heartbeat, not by ACK).
3. **Server→client replay buffer / retransmit-on-gap**: #117 wanted to replay `ack+1..lastSent`. The spec now **explicitly rejects retransmission** ("Acknowledgements and a retransmit queue are deliberately not part of the protocol"; recovery is always a full snapshot). So this is **rejected by design**, not just unimplemented.
4. **Client→server event loss / event sequence / retransmit unacked events**: This is the one genuinely unaddressed gap. Events sent into a half-open connection are dropped with no retransmit; the only recovery is the watchdog detecting the dead connection and reconnecting (but the events are gone). This remains real.

So the verdict: #117 is **still relevant only as a narrow problem statement** — client→server event delivery durability — and should be **rewritten/narrowed**; the ACK/replay design it proposes should be dropped or reconsidered because it contradicts the now-settled "stateless snapshot recovery, no ACK/retransmit" decision.

I should also consider: is even the client→server event-loss problem worth solving? The current mitigation: the client watchdog detects a dead connection within ~2 heartbeat intervals (10s? HEARTBEAT_TIMEOUT_MS) and reconnects + resyncs. But events (text/value) typed in that window are lost. For most inputs, the app state is reconstructed from... no, it's not — a lost TEXT_CHANGED means the server never sees the typed text. However, the DOM client is authoritative for the input element's value until the server echoes; if the server never got it, on reconnect the RESYNC would reset the field to the server's value, losing the typed text. So yes, real data loss.

But there might be an argument that this is acceptable / low priority for the POC. The issue is part of the "Enterprise SRE" milestone, so reliability matters.

## Problem

The web client's outbound raw-input events are fire-and-forget. `WebSocket.send()` is optimistic: when the connection is half-open (NAT/proxy drop, wedged send path) the browser reports success but the server never receives the batch, and neither side notices until the heartbeat watchdog (~2×5s) closes and reconnects. Events sent in that window are lost.

Concretely, a `TEXT_CHANGED`/`VALUE_CHANGED`/tap that lands in a silent-drop window never reaches the server. On reconnect the client requests `META::RESYNC`; the server re-renders its authoritative state, which then clobbers the user's uncommitted input (the typed text/committed value is gone). This is the inverse direction from the loss #58 fixed.

## Scope

**In scope:** durability of guest → host (client → server) raw-input events across a *silent* connection drop.

**Out of scope (settled):** server → client delta retransmit. `spec/OPCODE.md` §Sequence gap detection explicitly rejects ACKs/replay buffers for server deltas; recovery there is a full `META::RESYNC` snapshot. Do not reintroduce ACK for the host → guest direction.

## Constraints

- The renderer/host remains stateless; the application owns state. Recovery must not require the server to retain per-event history beyond a bounded, idempotent window.
- Events are idempotent (a tap, a text/value set) — re-applying an event is safe.
- Must not conflict with the heartbeat (`META::PING`/`PONG`) or the existing sequence numbering (only guest → host *delta* batches consume a sequence; requests carry 0).

## Design options (to decide)

1. **Client-side unacked-event buffer + event sequence.** Stamp each guest → host event batch with a per-connection monotonic sequence (reuse/extend the batch header; only delta batches currently consume `sequence`). Buffer unacked events (latest-per-control, bounded); on reconnect resend unacked before/with `META::RESYNC`; server dedupes by sequence. Requires a server→client ACK (reintroduces an ACK — for the guest→host event direction only).
2. **Replay-on-reconnect without ACK.** Client keeps a small bounded tail of recent input events and, on reconnect (before RESYNC), resends the tail; server treats events idempotently. Simpler, no ACK, but over-sends and can't distinguish delivered vs not.
3. **Client-authoritative input recovery.** On RESYNC, the client re-applies its locally-held uncommitted input for the focused control after the snapshot lands (no server involvement). Avoids protocol change but is renderer-specific and doesn't cover non-focus events (taps/nav).

## Verification

- TS unit tests: events buffered while `connecting`/`reconnecting` are flushed on open; sequence stamped; resend-on-reconnect.
- Java tests: idempotent re-apply of a resent event.
- Live flaky-link check against the Quarkus demo.
- `status.md` updates for `lib/typescript`, `pathland-server-core`, and the spec if the wire changes.

Related: #58 (sequence gap detection + heartbeat), #114, #115.

## Summary

The web client's outbound raw-input events are **fire-and-forget**. `WebSocket.send()` is optimistic: on a half-open / silently-broken connection (NAT or proxy drop, wedged send path) the browser reports success while the server never receives the batch, and neither side notices until the heartbeat watchdog (~2×5 s) closes and reconnects. Any event sent in that window is lost.

Concretely, a `TEXT_CHANGED` / `VALUE_CHANGED` / tap that lands in a silent-drop window never reaches the server. On reconnect the client requests `META::RESYNC`; the server re-renders its authoritative state, which then clobbers the user's uncommitted input (the typed text / committed value is gone).

This is the **inverse direction** from the loss #58 fixed. #58 made *server → client* delta loss detectable (batch `sequence` gap → `META::RESYNC`) and added the heartbeat; the *client → server* event path is still silent.

## Scope

**In scope:** durability of guest → host (client → server) raw-input events across a **silent** connection drop.

**Out of scope (settled):** server → client delta retransmit. `spec/OPCODE.md` §Sequence gap detection explicitly rejects ACKs and a retransmit queue for server deltas — recovery there is always a full `META::RESYNC` snapshot. Do **not** reintroduce ACK for the host → guest direction.

## Constraints

- The renderer/host stays stateless; the application owns state. Recovery must not require the server to retain unbounded per-event history.
- Raw-input events are idempotent (a tap, a text/value set) — re-applying one is safe.
- Must not conflict with the heartbeat (`META::PING`/`PONG`) or with the existing `sequence` rule (only guest → host *delta* batches consume a sequence; requests carry `0`).

## Design options (to decide)

1. **Client-side unacked-event buffer + event sequence.** Stamp each guest → host event batch with a per-connection monotonic sequence (extend the batch-header sequencing rule to event batches), buffer unacked events (latest-per-control, bounded), resend unacked on reconnect, server dedupes by sequence. Requires a server → client ACK — reintroduces ACK **only** for the guest → host event direction.
2. **Replay-on-reconnect without ACK.** The client keeps a small bounded tail of recent input events and, on reconnect (before `META::RESYNC`), resends the tail; the server treats events idempotently. Simpler, no ACK, but over-sends and cannot distinguish delivered from not.
3. **Client-authoritative input recovery.** On `META::RESYNC` the client re-applies its locally-held uncommitted input for the focused control after the snapshot lands (no server involvement, no protocol change). Renderer-specific and does not cover non-focus events (taps / navigation).

## Verification

- TS unit tests: events issued while `connecting`/`reconnecting` are buffered and flushed on open; event sequence stamped; resend-on-reconnect.
- Java tests: idempotent re-apply of a resent event does not double-apply.
- Live flaky-link check against the Quarkus demo.
- `status.md` updates for `lib/typescript`, `pathland-server-core`, and the spec if the wire format changes.

Related: #58 (sequence gap detection + heartbeat, closed), #114 (Quarkus send-failure-close), #115 (delta batching). Supersedes the ACK/replay-buffer design of #117.

"Closing as **done** — the goal (coalesce outbound frames into one PLPL batch under a time/size policy, no per-frame WS messages) is implemented, and more broadly than this issue scoped it.

- `DeltaBatcher` (`pathland-server-core`) merges session delta frames (opcodes + a single rebased string section) and flushes on a timer/byte threshold. It's wired into every session (`PathlandSession`), so **both** demos get it — not just the demos, which is what this issue asked for.
- Covered by `DeltaBatcherTest`: merge + string-offset rebasing, a 100-frame drag burst collapsing to one send, incrementing batch sequences (empty flush consumes none), and a blocking sender not holding the lock.
- The issue's premise ('outbound frames are sent one WS message per frame') is stale.

Note on the policy: the Java defaults are **20 ms / 16 KB**, not the Rust `Batcher`'s **4 ms / 1400 B**. That difference is intentional — 20 ms (~50 flushes/s) suits a remote WebSocket, whereas the Rust policy targets the shared-memory ring; 4 ms over a WS would send nearly every frame. If cross-transport parity is ever wanted, the MTU-friendly 1400 B half is the defensible part to adopt — but there's no functional gap today."

wire format and APIs may change before 1.0.

[![CI](https://github.com/PathlandDev/Pathland/actions/workflows/ci.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/PathlandDev/Pathland/actions/workflows/ci.yml)

## Pathland is a protocol

Pathland is first and foremost a **binary UI protocol** — not just a framework,
and not a single rendering
target. Your view declaration compiles to fixed 16-byte opcodes that any renderer
applies to native elements. The wire is the contract: a view written in Java, Rust,
C#, or anything else produces the **same opcode stream**, and any renderer can
apply it.

That makes Pathland **language- and renderer-agnostic**:

- **Write the UI once, declaratively.** A SwiftUI-shaped DSL in your language of
  choice — Java, Rust, C#, anything — describes the same view structure, whatever
  it later runs on.
- **Run it on any surface.** The same view code drives today's server-rendered web
  and the native GTK4 desktop renderer, and is on track for the browser via WASM,
  embedded chips (LVGL), and native mobile/desktop (SwiftUI/UIKit, Jetpack Compose,
  Qt) ([Where it's headed](#where-its-headed)).
- **Only changes travel.** The protocol is a stream of tiny binary deltas: an
  unchanged screen transmits zero bytes, and updates are applied in place.

**Server-side rendering is the first surface we ship** — the flagship
getting-started path — **not the whole story**. It's the on-ramp that's useful
today; the protocol underneath is where the portability comes from.

## The flagship path today: SSR

The fastest way to replace a BFF + JavaScript-frontend stack. You write the **whole
UI in your backend language** — Java, C#, Rust, anything. Pathland renders the first
page as server-side HTML, so it appears instantly, then keeps it alive with tiny
binary updates over a WebSocket. The result is a smooth, reactive UI — delivered by

The HtmlRenderer extracts `/META-INF/native/...` from the jar resource. When running from target/classes (not a jar), the resource `/META-INF/native/libpathland_render_html.dylib` would be in `pathland-render-html/target/classes/META-INF/native/`. `mvn install` (which I ran) would have re-embedded the fresh dylib into `target/classes/META-INF/native/` (the antrun runs at process-resources, copying to `project.build.outputDirectory` = target/classes). So after my mvn install, `target/classes/META-INF/native/libpathland_render_html.dylib` should be fresh!

But the RUNNING instance (PID 99579) started at 8:51 AM — BEFORE my mvn install (09:21). So it's running with the OLD dylib extracted (from before). And it's been running since 8:51, so my curl hit THIS process, which has the stale dylib loaded in memory.

Committed `c534f290` on `fix/zstack-grid-minmax` (user's `MusicPlayerView.java` left uncommitted).

## What was done

**Root cause:** `z-index` was emitted on the child element *inside* the `grid-area:1/1` shell. CSS only honors `z-index` on positioned/flex/grid items — the child is a plain block, so it was inert, and the shell (the actual grid item) had no z-index → overlapping ZStack siblings stacked purely by DOM order.

**Fix:**
- **SSR** (`pathland-render-html`): a `Z_INDEX != 0` on a ZStack child / grid cell is now emitted on its **shell** (`grid-area:1/1;z-index:N;…`); the child keeps its own (the client reads it).
- **DOM client**: `applyLayout` copies a child/cell's `z-index` onto its shell each pass (ZStack branch + grid `setShell`), mirroring SSR.
- **Bonus bug found:** `classes.ts` decoded Z_INDEX via `u32(bits)` but the wire type is **F32** (per `value_type_for`/`ValueTypes.forProperty`) — float bits read raw gave huge z-values and broke negatives. Now `Math.round(f32(vt, c))`.
- **Spec**: `PRIMITIVES.md` §ZStack + `MODIFIERS.md` define Z_INDEX as a draw-order override (higher = on top, equal → child index).

**Verified:** new Rust + TS tests (shell carries `z-index:5`, sibling shell empty, F32/negative decode); 192 TS + full Rust suite green; goldens unchanged.

Done. **`4204ca3f`** on `fix/zstack-grid-minmax`.

## The Safari fix

**Root cause:** on WebKit, overlapping grid items with differing `align-self` (the library `stretch` vs the player bar `end`) paint in the wrong order when every shell is `z-index:auto` — so the library's buttons drew above the player bar. Chrome/FF follow the spec.

- ZStack container: `isolation:isolate` → a stacking context, keeping the shells' z-indexes scoped inside the ZStack.
- Every ZStack child shell: explicit `z-index` — the child's `Z_INDEX`, else `0`. Two stacking-context boxes at equal z-index paint in tree order per spec in *every* browser, so the player bar always draws above the library content; an explicit `Z_INDEX` still wins.

Now let me analyze the flicker precisely and design the fix.

The SRT cues are a ROLLING WINDOW: each cue shows ~2-4 accumulated lines, drops the oldest, adds one new (last). E.g., Across:
- Cue 1: [A, B]
- Cue 2: [A, B, C]
- Cue 3: [B, C, D]
- Cue 4: [C, D, E]

The proportional-over-all-lines within each cue:
- Cue 1: A (0-1.6), B (1.6-3.2)
- Cue 2: A (3.2-4.27), B (4.27-5.33), C (5.33-6.4)
- Cue 3: B (6.4-7.47), C (7.47-8.53), D (8.53-9.6)

Display sequence: A, B, A, B, C, B, C, D → the A↔B back-and-forth the user sees. Confirmed root cause.

The line being sung: each cue's NEW (last) line is the current lyric. So the correct monotonic display = the LAST non-empty line of the covering cue:
- Cue 1 → B, Cue 2 → C, Cue 3 → D, ... → monotonic B, C, D, E, F. No flicker.

So the fix is to revert `lineAt` to return the last non-empty line of the covering cue (the new line for that cue's window), which is monotonic and stable.

But the user's earlier complaint about that exact approach ("shows the next line instead of the current line")... Let me reconcile. With the rolling window, the LAST line of the covering cue is the line being sung in that window. So it IS the current line. The user's "next line" perception might have come from the FIRST cue (cue 1 has [A, B] — both new — and showing B for the whole 3.2s means A never shows). Or the user saw the very first cue show B while A was being sung.

Hmm — to be safe and address BOTH concerns, I could present the fix as: **show the last non-empty line of the covering cue (monotonic), which is the line sung in that cue's window** — and explain that the earlier "next line" impression likely came from the first cue / the window granularity, and that per-line precision isn't in the SRT data.

Actually — let me reconsider offering the alternative: show the FULL cue block. But the user explicitly wanted a single line ("newest line only"). The flicker fix should keep single-line.

Let me present the plan:
1. Root cause: the proportional change distributes ALL of a cue's lines across its window, but consecutive karaoke cues overlap (rolling window), so at each boundary the display restarts at an earlier line → A, B, A, B, C oscillation.
2. Fix: `Lyrics.lineAt` returns the **last non-empty line of the covering cue** (the line newly sung in that cue's window) — monotonic across cues (B, C, D, ...), one line per cue window, no internal switching.
3. Tests: update LyricsTest to assert the newest-line semantics again (the displayed line at cue start == the cue's last non-empty cleaned line; and it changes monotonically across cues; advance-within-cue test removed/replaced).
4. Keep the italic (already committed).
5. Rebuild + verify + commit a follow-up on `feat/subtitle-lyrics`.

Let me also double-check: does the last-line-of-covering-cue produce the "current line" the user wants? During cue k, the newly-sung line is the last line of cue k. Yes. And it's monotonic. 

One more consideration — the user said "switches back and forth between 2 lines WHILE ONE LINE IS SUNG". So during the singing of a single line, it oscillates A↔B. The newest-line fix shows one constant line per window. ✓ addresses it.

Now — should I also consider that the user might prefer the display to lag so the line appears exactly when sung? Without per-line timing, the newest-line-per-window is the best. I'll note it.

Let me also reconsider: maybe present BOTH the recommended fix (newest line of covering cue) and the full-block option, and let the user pick. Given the user's history (they chose "newest line only" before), I'll recommend newest-line-of-covering-cue but mention the full-block alternative.

Actually — let me reconsider once more. The user's FIRST complaint ("next line instead of current") + the flicker now. If I revert to newest-line-of-covering-cue, they may re-raise the "next line" issue. Is there a fix that shows the current line with sub-cue precision WITHOUT flicker?

The rolling window gives a sequence of new lines L1, L2, L3... each sung during its cue's window [start_k, end_k). The display of L_k during [start_k, end_k) is the accurate current line (given the data). The user's "next line" perception: maybe because the FIRST cue shows B immediately, and B is sung partway through. To fix the "early" appearance, we could show the new line only during the LAST portion of its window and show the PREVIOUS line during the earlier portion — but that requires knowing per-line sub-intervals.

Actually — here's a cleaner idea: **the new line of cue k is sung during cue k's window, but the PREVIOUS new line (L_{k-1}) continues to be the current line until the new line actually starts.** In karaoke, the new line starts at the cue boundary (end_k = start_{k+1}). So L_k is current during [start_k, end_k). Showing L_k for the whole window is correct. The "early" perception was likely just the first cue.

I'll go with newest-line-of-covering-cue as the recommended fix, explain it clearly, and offer the full-block alternative. Let me present.

Let me also confirm the exact new lineAt (revert):
```java
public static String lineAt(String title, float seconds) {
    for (Cue cue : cuesFor(title)) {
        if (seconds >= cue.start() && seconds < cue.end()) {
            List<String> lines = cue.lines();
            for (int i = lines.size() - 1; i >= 0; i--) {
                String clean = clean(lines.get(i));
                if (!clean.isEmpty()) {
                    return clean;
                }
            }
        }
    }
    return "";
}
```
This is exactly the original (approach 1). Monotonic.

Confirmed: `bb6e18b8` committed (proportional + italic), tree clean. Here's the diagnosis and plan.

## Root cause of the flicker

The karaoke SRTs are a **rolling window**, not strict accumulation — each cue shows ~2–4 lines, drops the oldest, and adds one new *last* line (Across: `[A,B] → [A,B,C] → [B,C,D] → [C,D,E]`). My proportional change distributes **all** of a cue's lines across its window, so each cue *restarts at line 0*:

```
cue1: A, B | cue2: A, B, C | cue3: B, C, D →  A, B, A, B, C, B, C, D
```

That A↔B oscillation is exactly the "switches back and forth between 2 lines while one line is sung."

## Plan — make it monotonic

The line being sung in cue *k*'s window is its **new (last) line**, so the correct stable display is the **last non-empty line of the covering cue** — it advances monotonically (`B, C, D, E, …`), one constant line per window, no internal switching.

1. **`Lyrics.lineAt`**: revert the proportional logic to return the last non-empty cleaned line of the covering cue (the new line for that window).
2. **`LyricsTest`**:
   - a cue's displayed line == its last non-empty cleaned line, constant across the window (no switching);
   - consecutive cues advance monotonically (cue *k*'s line ≠ cue *k+1*'s line);
   - keep the missing-file / out-of-range / new-tracks tests.
3. **Verify + commit**: `mvn test -pl pathland-demo-views`, rebuild/repackage the Spring demo, curl the SSR, commit a follow-up on `feat/subtitle-lyrics`. (The italic styling stays — already in.)

**Note on the earlier "next line" impression:** with per-cue windows this is the most faithful "current line" the SRT data can give (there's no per-line timing in the files). If you'd rather see the full current chorus block (all of the cue's lines, karaoke-style, multi-line pill), I can do that instead — it's also monotonic and flicker-free.

Yes — these SRT files ARE karaoke-style formatted. Each cue contains a rolling block of 2-4 accumulated lines with the new line appended. In karaoke subtitles (like Apple Music's animated lyrics or typical karaoke video), the display shows the FULL current block, with the current line highlighted (e.g., bold/colored) and the others dimmed. That's what the format is designed for — the accumulated block provides context (the repeated chorus) while the newest line is the one being sung.

So "karaoke style with multiple lines" is indeed what the cues are formatted for. And it's flicker-free (the block rolls forward). The BEST karaoke display would:
- Show the current cue's full block (multi-line).
- Highlight the CURRENT (newest) line (e.g., white/bright) while the earlier lines are dimmed (translucent white or a secondary color).
- Advance monotonically.

But our earlier single-line approach was simpler. Given the user is now leaning toward karaoke style, and it's genuinely what the format is for, I should recommend it and plan it.

However — there's a nuance: the pill is a single Text node. For karaoke multi-line with per-line styling (highlight current line, dim others), I'd need either:
- A VStack of Text nodes (one per line), each styled (current = white, others = dimmed), OR
- A single Text with the block joined by newlines (no per-line highlight).

/** The karaoke lyric pill just above the floating player bar: the current
 *  cue's block in italic — the newest (last) line bright white, the earlier
 *  chorus lines dimmed — on a translucent black pill; invisible (clear) when
 *  there is no block. Taps pass through. */
private static View subtitlePill(Signal<List<String>> block) {
    List<View> rows = new ArrayList<>();
    for (int i = 0; i < MAX_LYRICS_LINES; i++) {
        int index = i;
        rows.add(Text.of(computed(() -> lineAt(block.get(), index)))
                .with(FontSize.of(13))
                .with(FontStyleMod.of(FontStyle.ITALIC))
                .with(ForegroundStyle.of(computed(() -> index == block.get().size() - 1
                        ? Color.WHITE
                        : Color.argb(170, 255, 255, 255)))));
    }
    return VStack.of(HorizontalAlignment.CENTER, 2, rows.toArray(View[]::new))
            .with(Padding.of(6, 12, 6, 12))
            .with(CornerRadius.of(8))
            .with(Offset.of(0, -(BAR_HEIGHT + 24)))
            .with(AllowsHitTesting.of(false))
            .with(Background.of(computed(() -> block.get().isEmpty()
                    ? Color.CLEAR
                    : Color.argb(128, 0, 0, 0))));
}

/** The row text for a block index (empty beyond the block). */
private static String lineAt(List<String> block, int i) {
    return i < block.size() ? block.get(i) : "";
}

## The fix

The instability came from the current-line sweep: it swept the **whole rolling block**, which restarts at each cue boundary — so the current line (and the previous line above it) jumped back to repeated chorus text and oscillated while a line was sung.

`Lyrics.currentIndex` now sweeps **only the lines the covering cue actually adds** (computed via the longest suffix-of-previous = prefix-of-current overlap):
- first cue → sweeps its whole block (all lines are new);
- rolling cues (the common case) → the single new line is **constant** for the whole window;
- hold cues (no new lines) → keep the newest line.

So the pair is monotonic and stable — `(A,B), (B,C), (C,D), …` — the pill holds two steady lines, with the current (bottom) white and the previous (top) dimmed, exactly as you asked.

**Verified:** 27 demo-views tests green (current sweeps the first cue, a rolling cue holds its line across the window, `previousLine` spans boundaries, empty only at the very first line); the served SSR carries the two-row italic pill. Restart the app and play — the previous line should now sit still instead of switching up and down.

Found it — `previousLine` still computes its `current` with the **old whole-block proportional math** (`(int)(t*n)`), not the new-lines sweep that `currentIndex` uses. - The seek is **change-gated**: `should_seek` is evaluated only when the target changed since the last read; the retained value re-read every reconcile is a no-op. Real seeks (a changed target, e.g. a slider drag) still fire; the echo guard still suppresses `MEDIA_TIME_UPDATED` echoes.

A `GtkScale`'s own drag gesture was consuming the button release, so the renderer's `GestureClick::released` never fired → the drag session (and in-flight suppression) stayed active → the app's seek-on-release never committed → audio stayed old.

Now each **user `value-changed` during a slider drag re-arms a ~150 ms timer**; when the drag settles, the timer clears the session and reports `EDITING_CHANGED(false)` — guaranteeing the commit (and thus the seek) fires even without a release signal. `GestureClick::released` remains the immediate path when it does fire; the settle is a no-op fallback (it checks `drag_state`, so it never double-emits).

OUT = pathlib.Path("/Users/michael/Development/michaelkrog/Pathland/docs/prompts-all-sessions.md")

con = sqlite3.connect(f"file:{DB}?mode=ro", uri=True)
cur = con.cursor()

sessions = cur.execute(
    """SELECT id, title, time_created FROM session
       WHERE project_id=? AND title NOT LIKE '%(@explore subagent)%' AND title NOT LIKE 'Pipa Huddle%'
       ORDER BY time_created""",
    (PROJECT,),
).fetchall()

def date_of(ts_ms):
    return datetime.datetime.fromtimestamp(ts_ms / 1000).strftime("%Y-%m-%d")

def prompts_for(session_id):
    rows = cur.execute(
        """SELECT json_extract(p.data,'$.text') AS t, m.time_created, p.time_created
           FROM part p JOIN message m ON m.id=p.message_id
           WHERE m.session_id=? AND json_extract(m.data,'$.role')='user'
             AND json_extract(p.data,'$.type')='text'
           ORDER BY m.time_created, p.time_created""",
        (session_id,),
    ).fetchall()
    out = []
    cur_msg = None
    buf = []
    for text, mt, pt in rows:
        if not text or not str(text).strip():
            continue
        if mt != cur_msg:
            if cur_msg is not None:
                out.append("\n".join(buf))
            cur_msg = mt
            buf = [str(text)]
        else:

    if cur_msg is not None:
        out.append("\n".join(buf))
    return out

lines.append("")
lines.append("**Generated:** October 4, 2026")

lines.append("")

# Section 0: today's session from the existing file.
today_items = []
if TODAY_MD.exists():
    body = TODAY_MD.read_text()
    in_list = False
    for ln in body.splitlines():
        m = re.match(r"^(\d+)\.\s+(.*)$", ln)
        if m:
            in_list = True
            today_items.append(f"{m.group(1)}. {m.group(2)}")
        elif in_list and ln.strip() == "":

        elif in_list:
            # continuation line of a multi-line prompt item
            today_items[-1] += "\n" + ln
        # skip the header block (before the list starts)

lines.append("")

for idx, (sid, title, ts) in enumerate(sessions, start=1):
    prompts = prompts_for(sid)
    lines.append(f"## {date_of(ts)} — {title}")
    lines.append("")
    if not prompts:

    else:
        for i, p in enumerate(prompts, start=1):
            lines.append(f"{i}. {p}")
            lines.append("")
    lines.append("")

OUT.write_text("\n".join(lines))
print(f"wrote {OUT}")
print(f"historical main sessions: {len(sessions)}")
total = len(today_items) + sum(len(prompts_for(s[0])) for s in sessions)
print(f"total prompts (today {len(today_items)} + historical {total - len(today_items)}): {total}")

import pathlib, re

FILE = pathlib.Path("/Users/michael/Development/michaelkrog/Pathland/docs/prompts-all-sessions.md")
BARE = re.compile(
    r"^(go|yes|ok|okay|yeah|yep|yup|y|sure|continue|proceed|go ahead|do it|fine|great|lgtm|sounds good|ok go|yes go|perfect|awesome|roger|got it|understood|agree)([.!]*)$",
    re.IGNORECASE,
)

def clean_item(text):
    """Strip today's editorial annotations; return a list of raw prompts (0..n)."""
    # 'go  — *close #59 as done*' / 'yes  — *check that main builds/tests green*'
    text = re.sub(r"\s+—\s+\*[^*]*\*$", "", text)
    # 'Is %9 still relevant → *"I meant #59"*' -> split into two raw prompts
    m = re.match(r"^(.*?)\s+→\s+\*\"?([^*\"]*)\"?\*$", text)
    if m:
        return [p.strip() for p in (m.group(1), m.group(2)) if p.strip()]
    # trailing '(included a pasted SSR HTML attachment)'
    text = re.sub(r"\s+\(included a pasted SSR HTML attachment\)\*?\s*$", "", text)
    # '*Design answers:* ... (Recommended)' -> drop the editorial framing
    text = re.sub(r"^\*Design answer\(s\)?:\*\s*", "", text)
    text = re.sub(r"\s+\(Recommended\)\s*$", "", text)
    text = text.strip()
    return [] if BARE.match(text) else [text]

lines = FILE.read_text().splitlines()
out = []
i = 0
removed = 0
while i < len(lines):
    ln = lines[i]
    out.append(ln)
    i += 1
    if ln.startswith("## 2026-10-04 — this session"):
        # consume the section: numbered items + their indented continuations
        items = []
        while i < len(lines) and not lines[i].startswith("## "):
            if re.match(r"^\d+\.\s", lines[i]):
                items.append(re.sub(r"^\d+\.\s+", "", lines[i]))
            elif lines[i].startswith("   ") and items:
                items[-1] += "\n" + lines[i][3:]
            i += 1
        # process
        cleaned = []
        for raw in items:
            for p in clean_item(raw):
                if BARE.match(p.strip()):
                    removed += 1
                else:
                    cleaned.append(p.strip())
        num = 0
        for text in cleaned:
            parts = text.splitlines()
            num += 1
            out.append(f"{num}. {parts[0]}")
            for rest in parts[1:]:
                out.append(f"   {rest}")
            out.append("")
        out.append("")
        removed_today = 48 - len(cleaned)
        print(f"today's section: 48 -> {len(cleaned)} prompts (removed {48 - len(cleaned)})")

FILE.write_text("\n".join(out) + "\n")
print(f"rewrote {FILE}")

import sqlite3, datetime, pathlib, re

DB = pathlib.Path.home() / ".local/share/opencode/opencode.db"
PROJECT = "f6fb094b3c5af4dd70729bfbc028ad0777169d11"
TODAY_MD = pathlib.Path("/Users/michael/Development/michaelkrog/Pathland/docs/session-prompts-2026-10-04.md")
OUT = pathlib.Path("/Users/michael/Development/michaelkrog/Pathland/docs/prompts-all-sessions.md")
LONG_SESSION = "Pathland layout specs next steps"  # the Oct 1 session that continued into today

BARE = re.compile(
    r"^(go|yes|ok|okay|yeah|yep|yup|y|sure|continue|proceed|go ahead|do it|fine|great|lgtm|sounds good|ok go|yes go|perfect|awesome|roger|got it|understood|agree)([.!]*)$",
    re.IGNORECASE,
)

def clean_item(text):
    """Strip today's editorial annotations; return a list of raw prompts (0..n)."""
    text = re.sub(r"\s+—\s+\*[^*]*\*$", "", text)
    m = re.match(r"^(.*?)\s+→\s+\*\"?([^*\"]*)\"?\*$", text)
    if m:
        return [p.strip() for p in (m.group(1), m.group(2)) if p.strip()]
    text = re.sub(r"\s+\*?\((included a pasted SSR HTML attachment|repeated)\)\*?\s*$", "", text)
    text = re.sub(r"^\*Design answers?:\*\s*", "", text)
    text = re.sub(r"\s+\(Recommended\)\s*$", "", text)
    text = text.strip()
    return [] if BARE.match(text) else [text]

def fmt_item(num, p):
    lines = p.splitlines() or [""]
    out = [f"{num}. {lines[0]}"]
    for ln in lines[1:]:
        out.append(f"   {ln}" if ln else "")
    return "\n".join(out)

# ---- today's prompts from the file ----
today = []
body = TODAY_MD.read_text()
cur = None
for ln in body.splitlines():
    m = re.match(r"^(\d+)\.\s+(.*)$", ln)
    if m:
        if cur is not None:
            today.append(cur)
        cur = m.group(2)
    elif cur is not None and ln.startswith(" "):
        cur += "\n" + ln.strip()
    elif cur is not None and ln.strip() == "":
        continue
if cur is not None:
    today.append(cur)
today_clean = []
for raw in today:
    for p in clean_item(raw):
        today_clean.append(p)

con = sqlite3.connect(f"file:{DB}?mode=ro", uri=True)
cur = con.cursor()
sessions = cur.execute(
    """SELECT id, title, time_created FROM session
       WHERE project_id=? AND title NOT LIKE '%(@explore subagent)%' AND title NOT LIKE 'Pipa Huddle%'
       ORDER BY time_created""",
    (PROJECT,),
).fetchall()
others = [s for s in sessions if s.title != LONG_SESSION]
long_s = [s for s in sessions if s.title == LONG_SESSION]

def date_of(ts_ms):
    return datetime.datetime.fromtimestamp(ts_ms / 1000).strftime("%Y-%m-%d")

def prompts_for(session_id, before=None):
    where = "m.session_id=?"
    args = [session_id]
    if before is not None:
        where += " AND datetime(m.time_created/1000,'unixepoch') < ?"
        args.append(before)
    rows = cur.execute(
        f"""SELECT json_extract(p.data,'$.text') AS t, m.time_created, p.time_created
            FROM part p JOIN message m ON m.id=p.message_id
            WHERE {where} AND json_extract(m.data,'$.role')='user'
              AND json_extract(p.data,'$.type')='text'
            ORDER BY m.time_created, p.time_created""",
        args,
    ).fetchall()
    out, cur_msg, buf = [], None, []
    for text, mt, pt in rows:
        if not text or not str(text).strip():
            continue
        if mt != cur_msg:
            if cur_msg is not None:
                out.append("\n".join(buf))
            cur_msg, buf = mt, [str(text)]
        else:
            buf.append(str(text))
    if cur_msg is not None:
        out.append("\n".join(buf))
    return out

lines = []
lines.append("# Pathland — prompts across sessions")
lines.append("")
lines.append("**Generated:** October 4, 2026")
lines.append("**Scope:** all user prompts for the Pathland project across sessions. Main sessions only — the `@explore` subagent task prompts and the Pipa voice-huddle transcript are excluded. Source: the opencode session store (`~/.local/share/opencode/opencode.db`).")
lines.append("")

lines.append("## 2026-10-04 — this session")
lines.append("")
for i, p in enumerate(today_clean, start=1):
    lines.append(fmt_item(i, p))
    lines.append("")

for sid, title, ts in others:

n_today = len(today_clean)
n_hist = sum(len(prompts_for(s[0])) for s in others) + sum(len(prompts_for(s[0], before="2026-10-04")) for s in long_s)

print(f"today: {n_today}; historical: {n_hist}; total: {n_today + n_hist}")

import sqlite3, datetime, pathlib, re

DB = pathlib.Path.home() / ".local/share/opencode/opencode.db"
PROJECT = "f6fb094b3c5af4dd70729bfbc028ad0777169d11"
TODAY_MD = pathlib.Path("/Users/michael/Development/michaelkrog/Pathland/docs/session-prompts-2026-10-04.md")
OUT = pathlib.Path("/Users/michael/Development/michaelkrog/Pathland/docs/prompts-all-sessions.md")
LONG_SESSION = "Pathland layout specs next steps"

BARE = re.compile(
    r"^(go|yes|ok|okay|yeah|yep|yup|y|sure|continue|proceed|go ahead|do it|fine|great|lgtm|sounds good|ok go|yes go|perfect|awesome|roger|got it|understood|agree)([.!]*)$",
    re.IGNORECASE,
)

def clean_item(text):
    text = re.sub(r"\s+—\s+\*[^*]*\*$", "", text)
    m = re.match(r"^(.*?)\s+→\s+\*\"?([^*\"]*)\"?\*$", text)
    if m:
        return [p.strip() for p in (m.group(1), m.group(2)) if p.strip()]
    text = re.sub(r"\s+\*?\((included a pasted SSR HTML attachment|repeated)\)\*?\s*$", "", text)
    text = re.sub(r"^\*Design answers?:\*\s*", "", text)
    text = re.sub(r"\s+\(Recommended\)\s*$", "", text)
    text = text.strip()
    return [] if BARE.match(text) else [text]

def fmt_item(num, p):
    lines = p.splitlines() or [""]
    out = [f"{num}. {lines[0]}"]
    for ln in lines[1:]:
        out.append(f"   {ln}" if ln else "")
    return "\n".join(out)

def norm(s):
    return re.sub(r"\s+", " ", s).strip()

# ---- parse today's file (raw items) ----
today = []
cur = None
for ln in TODAY_MD.read_text().splitlines():
    m = re.match(r"^(\d+)\.\s+(.*)$", ln)
    if m:
        if cur is not None:
            today.append(cur)
        cur = m.group(2)
    elif cur is not None and ln.startswith(" "):
        cur += "\n" + ln.strip()
if cur is not None:
    today.append(cur)
today_file_clean = []
for raw in today:
    today_file_clean.extend(clean_item(raw))

# ---- DB sessions ----
con = sqlite3.connect(f"file:{DB}?mode=ro", uri=True)
cur = con.cursor()
sessions = cur.execute(
    """SELECT id, title, time_created FROM session
       WHERE project_id=? AND title NOT LIKE '%(@explore subagent)%' AND title NOT LIKE 'Pipa Huddle%'
       ORDER BY time_created""",
    (PROJECT,),
).fetchall()
others = [s for s in sessions if s[1] != LONG_SESSION]
long_s = [s for s in sessions if s[1] == LONG_SESSION]

def date_of(ts_ms):
    return datetime.datetime.fromtimestamp(ts_ms / 1000).strftime("%Y-%m-%d")

def prompts_for(session_id, before=None, after=None):
    where = "m.session_id=?"
    args = [session_id]
    if before is not None:
        where += " AND datetime(m.time_created/1000,'unixepoch') < ?"
        args.append(before)
    if after is not None:
        where += " AND datetime(m.time_created/1000,'unixepoch') >= ?"
        args.append(after)
    rows = cur.execute(
        f"""SELECT json_extract(p.data,'$.text') AS t, m.time_created, p.time_created
            FROM part p JOIN message m ON m.id=p.message_id
            WHERE {where} AND json_extract(m.data,'$.role')='user'
              AND json_extract(p.data,'$.type')='text'
            ORDER BY m.time_created, p.time_created""",
        args,
    ).fetchall()
    out, cur_msg, buf = [], None, []
    for text, mt, pt in rows:
        if not text or not str(text).strip():
            continue
        if mt != cur_msg:
            if cur_msg is not None:
                out.append("\n".join(buf))
            cur_msg, buf = mt, [str(text)]
        else:
            buf.append(str(text))
    if cur_msg is not None:
        out.append("\n".join(buf))
    return out

# ---- today's section: file's pre-"Lets look at zstack" items + DB today verbatim ----
cut = next((i for i, p in enumerate(today_file_clean) if norm(p).startswith("Lets look at zstack")), len(today_file_clean))
early = today_file_clean[:cut]
db_today = []
for sid, title, ts in long_s:
    for raw in prompts_for(sid, before="2026-10-05", after="2026-10-04"):
        for p in clean_item(raw):
            if p.strip() and not BARE.match(norm(p)):
                db_today.append(p.strip())
today_clean = early + db_today

# ---- assemble ----
lines = ["# Pathland — prompts across sessions", "",
         "**Generated:** October 4, 2026",
         "**Scope:** all user prompts for the Pathland project across sessions. Main sessions only — the `@explore` subagent task prompts and the Pipa voice-huddle transcript are excluded. Today's (October 4) session is at the top: its early prompts were compacted out of the session store and survive in the session's own record, the rest are taken verbatim from the store. Source: the opencode session store (`~/.local/share/opencode/opencode.db`).",
         ""]

def emit_section(title, prompts):
    lines.append(title)
    lines.append("")
    if not prompts:
        lines.append("_(no user prompts)_")
        lines.append("")
        return
    for i, p in enumerate(prompts, start=1):
        lines.append(fmt_item(i, p))
        lines.append("")

emit_section("## 2026-10-04 — this session", today_clean)
for sid, title, ts in others:
    emit_section(f"## {date_of(ts)} — {title}", prompts_for(sid))
for sid, title, ts in long_s:
    emit_section(f"## {date_of(ts)} — {title}", prompts_for(sid, before="2026-10-04"))

OUT.write_text("\n".join(lines) + "\n")
print(f"wrote {OUT}")
print(f"today: {len(today_clean)}; historical: {sum(len(prompts_for(s[0])) for s in others) + sum(len(prompts_for(s[0], before='2026-10-04')) for s in long_s)}")
con.close()

12: Pathland is first and foremost a **binary UI protocol** — not just a framework,
13: and not a single rendering
14: target. Your view declaration compiles to fixed 16-byte opcodes that any renderer
15: applies to native elements. The wire is the contract: a view written in Java, Rust,
16: C#, or anything else produces the **same opcode stream**, and any renderer can
17: apply it.
18: 
19: That makes Pathland **language- and renderer-agnostic**:
20: 
21: - **Write the UI once, declaratively.** A SwiftUI-shaped DSL in your language of
22:   choice — Java, Rust, C#, anything — describes the same view structure, whatever
23:   it later runs on.
24: - **Run it on any surface.** The same view code drives today's server-rendered web
25:   and the native GTK4 desktop renderer, and is on track for the browser via WASM,
26:   embedded chips (LVGL), and native mobile/desktop (SwiftUI/UIKit, Jetpack Compose,
27:   Qt) ([Where it's headed](#where-its-headed)).
28: - **Only changes travel.** The protocol is a stream of tiny binary deltas: an
29:   unchanged screen transmits zero bytes, and updates are applied in place.
30: 
31: **Server-side rendering is the first surface we ship** — the flagship
32: getting-started path — **not the whole story**. It's the on-ramp that's useful
33: today; the protocol underneath is where the portability comes from.
34: 
35: ## The flagship path today: SSR
36: 
37: The fastest way to replace a BFF + JavaScript-frontend stack. You write the **whole
38: UI in your backend language** — Java, C#, Rust, anything. Pathland renders the first
39: page as server-side HTML, so it appears instantly, then keeps it alive with tiny
40: binary updates over a WebSocket. The result is a smooth, reactive UI — delivered by
41: the backend team, without npm, bundlers, an extra build pipeline, or a separate
42: frontend.
43: 
44: ```
45: You declare the UI in your backend
46:         │
47:         ▼
48: The server renders it (HTML) and owns it
49:         │
50:         ▼
51: Only the things that change travel to the client
52:         │
53:         ▼
54: The client applies them to native elements (60FPS)
55: ```
56: 
57: - **You declare the UI** with a SwiftUI-shaped DSL — `VStack`, `Text`, `Button`,
58:   styling — right next to your business logic.
59: - **The server renders and owns it.** The first page is plain HTML (instant paint,
60:   SEO-friendly); the server keeps the authoritative copy of the UI.
61: - **Only changes travel.** A click, a signal update, a navigation — the server sends
62:   a few tiny binary bytes describing exactly what changed. An unchanged screen
63:   sends nothing. The client applies them to real native elements (browser DOM, GTK
64:   widgets), so the platform does the layout, animation, and accessibility.
65: 
66: ## The whole app
67: 
68: Add one dependency and one bean, and you have a working app.
69: 
70: **Spring Boot**
71: 
72: ```java
73: @SpringBootApplication
74: public class MyApp {
75:     public static void main(String[] args) { SpringApplication.run(MyApp.class, args); }
76: 
77:     @Bean
78:     PathlandApp pathlandApp() { return () -> new MyHomeView(); }
79: }
80: ```
81: 
82: **Quarkus**
83: 
84: ```java
85: @ApplicationScoped
86: public class MyApp implements PathlandApp {
87:     public View newRoot() { return new MyHomeView(); }
88: }
89: ```
90: 
91: `MyHomeView` is just Java views — the same code runs on both:
92: 
93: ```java
94: public final class MyHomeView implements View {
95: 
96:     State<Integer> count = new State<>(0);   // persisted per session, automatically
97: 
98:     @Override
99:     public View body() {
100:         return VStack.of(
101:                 Text.of(Signals.computed(() -> "Clicked " + count.get() + " times")),
102:                 Button.of("Click me", () -> count.update(v -> v + 1))
103:         ).with(Padding.of(24));
104:     }
105: }
106: ```
107: 
108: That's it — SSR at any path, live updates over `/ws`, per-session state.
109: *(Imports omitted: `com.pathland.server.PathlandApp`, `com.pathland.view.*`.)*
110: 
111: ## What it removes
112: 
113: Today's server team pays for a BFF, a client-side state model, a SPA framework, and
114: a JS build toolchain — all to render UI the server already owns. Pathland removes
115: that layer: the backend *is* the application. There is no frontend contract to
116: maintain, no client state model, and no JavaScript to write — and the same backend
117: code that serves the web can drive other renderers later.
118: 
119: ## Why it's smooth
120: 
121: Pathland is built for smooth 60FPS UIs:
122: 
123: - **Only changes are sent.** A screen that isn't changing transmits zero bytes.
124:   Updates are tiny binary deltas, not re-rendered pages or JSON trees.
125: - **Native elements, not a canvas.** The platform lays out and animates real
126:   elements — you get native layout, text rendering, and accessibility for free,
127:   whether those elements are DOM nodes or GTK widgets.
128: - **A thin client.** The web client is a small static file that hydrates the server
129:   HTML and applies updates in place. No framework, no virtual DOM, no re-render cost.
130: 
131: ## The part you don't write
132: 
133: The web client is a single prebuilt JavaScript file you copy into your static
134: resources. It's shipped, not maintained — all the real logic lives in your backend.
135: (There's also a native GTK renderer for desktop.)
136: 
137: ## Where it runs today
138: 
139: - **Web (SSR + live WebSocket deltas)** — Java, with Spring Boot and Quarkus
140:   starters and demos; the flagship getting-started path.
141: - **Native desktop (GTK4)** — a renderer driven by the same protocol, from both the
142:   Rust DSL and the shared Java demo views (`pathland-gtk-demo`).
143: 
144: Two surfaces, one protocol — the demos' shared views run under both without a
145: rewrite.
146: 
147: ## Where it's headed
148: 
149: The SSR path above is the on-ramp — the protocol isn't limited to it.
150: 
151: Write the app logic once, run it on embedded, mobile, desktop, and browser. Pathland
152: is an open protocol, so the same code that drives the server-rendered UI today can
153: also run on the device itself:
154: 
155: - **In the browser**, the app logic compiles to WASM, writes to a shared buffer, and the
156:   main thread is left to rendering alone.
157: - **On embedded devices**, the logic runs on one core while another core renders, with
158:   the ring buffer carrying the protocol between them — mapped onto a lightweight UI
159:   toolkit like LVGL.
160: - **On mobile and desktop**, the same logic drives native renderers — SwiftUI/UIKit on
161:   Apple platforms, Jetpack Compose on Android, Qt and GTK on desktop.
162: 
163: Wherever it runs, only tiny binary updates travel across the ring buffer and are applied
164: in place — nothing is re-rendered or serialized, which is what keeps the UI stutter-free,
165: even on small devices.
166: 
167: ## Try it
168: 
169: Each demo has a one-command launcher in [`scripts/`](./scripts/). Run one from the
170: repository root — it builds its own prerequisites (Rust dylibs, the Java reactor)
171: and launches:
172: 
173: | Script | Demo | What you get |
174: |--------|------|--------------|
175: | `./scripts/run-spring-demo.sh` | Spring Boot SSR + WebSocket | http://localhost:8080 |
176: | `./scripts/run-quarkus-demo.sh` | Quarkus SSR + WebSocket (hot reload) | http://localhost:8080 |
177: | `./scripts/run-rust-gtk-demo.sh` | Rust DSL → GTK4 desktop renderer | a native window |
178: | `./scripts/run-java-gtk-demo.sh` | Java DSL → GTK4 desktop renderer (the shared `SplitNavDemo`) | a native window |
179: 
180: ```bash
181: # e.g. the Spring Boot demo
182: ./scripts/run-spring-demo.sh
183: ```
184: 
185: Notes:
186: - The web demos need a JDK 17+ (the whole stack runs on every LTS from 17).
187: - The GTK demos need the GTK4 + libadwaita system libraries.
188: - On macOS the Java GTK demo hands GTK the main thread automatically
189:   (`-XstartOnFirstThread`); Linux needs nothing special.
190: 
191: The same commands without the scripts:
192: 
193: ```bash
194: # one-time: build the Rust HTML renderer (embedded in the jar), then the Java reactor
195: cd lib/rust && cargo build -p pathland-render-html
196: cd lib/java && mvn install
197: 
198: # Spring Boot demo
199: cd lib/java/pathland-spring-boot-demo
200: mvn -q package && java -jar target/pathland-spring-boot-demo-0.1.0.jar
201: # → http://localhost:8080
202: 
203: # Quarkus demo (dev mode with hot reload)
204: cd lib/java/pathland-quarkus-demo
205: mvn quarkus:dev
206: # → http://localhost:8080
207: 
208: # Same protocol, native GTK desktop renderer (no browser)
209: cd lib/rust && cargo run -p pathland-render-gtk-demo
210: 
211: # Same protocol via Java: the shared demo views (SplitNavDemo) under the GTK renderer
212: cd lib/rust && cargo build -p pathland-core-capi -p pathland-render-gtk
213: cd lib/java/pathland-gtk-demo
214: MAVEN_OPTS="-XstartOnFirstThread" mvn -q compile exec:java \
215:   -Dpathland.core.lib=$PWD/../../lib/rust/target/debug/libpathland_core.dylib \
216:   -Dpathland.gtk.lib=$PWD/../../lib/rust/target/debug/libpathland_gtk.dylib
217: # (macOS needs -XstartOnFirstThread; Linux can drop it)
218: ```
219: 
220: ## The technical details
221: 
222: This README is the *what*. The *how* — the wire protocol, the DSL contract, the
223: conformance vectors, and the implementation notes — lives in [`spec/`](./spec/):
224: 
225: - [OPCODE.md](./spec/OPCODE.md) — the binary protocol
226: - [DSL.md](./spec/DSL.md) — the authoring surface (what you write)
227: - [PRIMITIVES.md](./spec/PRIMITIVES.md), [MODIFIERS.md](./spec/MODIFIERS.md), [EVENTS.md](./spec/EVENTS.md)
228: - [CONFORMANCE.md](./spec/CONFORMANCE.md) — golden byte vectors
229: 
230: ## Status & license
231: 
232: Proof of concept. See [CONTRIBUTING.md](./CONTRIBUTING.md),
233: [CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md](./CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md), [SECURITY.md](./SECURITY.md), and
234: [GENAI.md](./GENAI.md) (generative-AI transparency).
235: Licensed under the [Apache License 2.0](LICENSE).

16: /// consumers are granted short-lived `Guest`/`Host` views over the same buffer
17: /// via the borrowed methods, so opcodes flow in place with no copies.

## Root cause found and fixed

Your log showed it: Rust kept emitting events and waking Java, but **`[java] onEvent drain=0` every time** — the event ring had permanently deadlocked. 

**The bug** (`pathland-core/src/ring.rs:read_events` + `Host::frames`): both ring readers used a naive `write < read` guard. The masked write cursor eventually laps the read cursor numerically (wraps through 0) — once that happens, the reader bails with "empty" *without advancing its cursor*, the writer sits stuck "full", and **every subsequent drain returns 0 forever**. Exactly your symptoms: audio keeps playing, GTK hover keeps working, but no event ever reaches the app again. (There was even a test asserting the deadlock as intended behavior.)

**The fix**:
- Both rings now count the pending run **modulo the ring size** and drain across the wrap in ring order (`Host::frames` drains the wrapped head in one call, the tail in the next).
- Event drains take a `max` bound (`drain_event_opcodes_max`), so the C-ABI's 64-event buffer no longer drops events it can't copy.
- Replaced the deadlock tests with regression tests proving a wrapped producer drains correctly and can wrap again.
- `pathland-core/status.md` updated.

/// The renderer-owned default typography scale for a `TEXT_STYLE` code
/// (`spec/MODIFIERS.md` §2): `(size_pt, weight)`. `None` for an unknown code.
fn text_style_scale(code: u8) -> Option<(f32, f32)> {
    Some(match code {
        0 => (34.0, 700.0),  // LargeTitle
        1 => (28.0, 700.0),  // Title
        2 => (22.0, 700.0),  // Title2
        3 => (20.0, 600.0),  // Title3
        4 => (17.0, 600.0),  // Headline
        5 => (15.0, 400.0),  // Subheadline
        6 => (15.0, 400.0),  // Body
        7 => (14.0, 400.0),  // Callout
        8 => (13.0, 400.0),  // Footnote
        9 => (12.0, 400.0),  // Caption
        10 => (11.0, 400.0), // Caption2
        _ => return None,
    })
}

/// The generic CSS/Pango family for a `FONT_DESIGN` code.
fn font_design_family(code: u8) -> Option<&'static str> {
    match code {
        1 => Some("serif"),
        2 => Some("sans-serif"),
        3 => Some("monospace"),
        _ => None,
    }
}

# pathland-icons — implementation status

**Last updated:** October 6, 2026

The canonical icon catalog for the `ICON` primitive (spec/ICONS.md): a curated
set of neutral semantic names, single-sourced with their per-renderer native
mappings.

## Implemented

- **Catalog** (`CATALOG`): 48 entries, each `Icon(name, gtk, lucide_id, svg)`.
- **GTK mapping** (`gtk_icon_name`): Adwaita/freedesktop **symbolic** icon-theme
  names.
- **Lucide mapping + SVG data** (`lucide_id` / `lucide_svg` / `LUCIDE_SVG_OPEN` /
  `LUCIDE_SVG_CLOSE`): inline SVG inner markup vendored from Lucide v1.52.0
  (ISC — see `THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md`); consumed by `pathland-render-html`
  (SSR) and `pathland-ts-codegen` (→ the DOM client's `generated/icons.ts`).
- **Lookup + fallbacks**: `lookup` / `is_canonical` / `gtk_fallback`
  (`image-missing`) / `web_fallback_svg` for app-authored names the catalog
  does not map.
- **`no_std`** const data only (no `alloc`).

## Not implemented / gaps

- Only 48 curated icons; extending = add a catalog row (+ Lucide SVG + GTK name)
  and regenerate — the mechanism is the point, not the breadth.
- GTK names are best-effort theme lookups; an unavailable name falls back to the
  icon theme's `image-missing`, never a broken render.

## Verified by

`cargo test -p pathland-icons` — every catalog entry resolves on every renderer,
canonical names are unique, unknown names resolve to fallbacks.

/**
 * The canonical icon vocabulary for the {@link Icon} primitive (spec/ICONS.md).
 * These neutral semantic names match {@code pathland-icons} (the Rust catalog);
 * each renderer maps them to its native icon set — Adwaita on GTK, Lucide on the
 * web. The {@code wire()} value is the canonical {@code ICON_NAME} string.
 */
public enum IconName {

    HOME("home"),
    SETTINGS("settings"),
    SEARCH("search"),
    MENU("menu"),
    CLOSE("close"),
    CHEVRON_LEFT("chevron-left"),
    CHEVRON_RIGHT("chevron-right"),
    CHEVRON_UP("chevron-up"),
    CHEVRON_DOWN("chevron-down"),
    ARROW_LEFT("arrow-left"),
    ARROW_RIGHT("arrow-right"),
    ADD("add"),
    REMOVE("remove"),
    CHECK("check"),
    EDIT("edit"),
    DELETE("delete"),
    SAVE("save"),
    SHARE("share"),
    DOWNLOAD("download"),
    UPLOAD("upload"),
    REFRESH("refresh"),
    PLAY("play"),
    PAUSE("pause"),
    STOP("stop"),
    SKIP_BACK("skip-back"),
    SKIP_FORWARD("skip-forward"),
    VOLUME("volume"),
    VOLUME_MUTE("volume-mute"),
    SHUFFLE("shuffle"),
    REPEAT("repeat"),
    INFO("info"),
    WARNING("warning"),
    ERROR("error"),
    SUCCESS("success"),
    HEART("heart"),
    STAR("star"),
    USER("user"),
    USERS("users"),
    LOCK("lock"),
    LOGOUT("logout"),
    BELL("bell"),
    FOLDER("folder"),
    FILE("file"),
    IMAGE("image"),
    MUSIC("music"),
    GRID("grid"),
    LIST("list"),
    FILTER("filter");

    private final String wire;

    IconName(String wire) {
        this.wire = wire;
    }

    /** The canonical {@code ICON_NAME} value (the shared protocol vocabulary). */
    public String wire() {
        return wire;
    }

/// The canonical icon vocabulary for [`Icon`] (mirrors `pathland-icons` +
/// spec/ICONS.md). Each renderer maps a name to its native icon set — Adwaita
/// on GTK, Lucide on the web. The `canonical()` value is the `ICON_NAME` wire
/// string.
#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq)]
pub enum IconName {
    Home,
    Settings,
    Search,
    Menu,
    Close,
    ChevronLeft,
    ChevronRight,
    ChevronUp,
    ChevronDown,
    ArrowLeft,

    Logout,
    Bell,
    Folder,
    File,
    Image,
    Music,
    Grid,
    List,
    Filter,
}

impl IconName {
    /// The canonical `ICON_NAME` value.
    pub const fn canonical(self) -> &'static str {

/// A semantic icon (the `ICON` primitive): a canonical [`IconName`] mapped by
/// each renderer to its native icon set (spec/ICONS.md). Size follows
/// [`FontSize`] (text-style symbol sizing); tint follows [`ForegroundStyle`].
#[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq)]
pub struct Icon {
    name: &'static str,
}

impl Icon {
    /// A semantic icon from the canonical catalog.
    pub const fn new(name: IconName) -> Self {
        Self {
            name: name.canonical(),
        }
    }
}

impl View for Icon {
    fn build(&self) -> Node {
        let mut node = plain_node(Component::Icon, Vec::new(), BTreeMap::new());
        node.string_properties
            .insert(property_id::ICON_NAME, String::from(self.name));
        node
    }
}

/// A semantic icon (shorthand for [`Icon::new`]).
pub const fn icon(name: IconName) -> Icon {
    Icon::new(name)
}
