# Icons — the `ICON` primitive and canonical vocabulary

The `ICON` primitive (0x0B) renders a **renderer-native symbol** for a canonical,
semantic name written once in the UI model. Unlike `IMAGE` (an asset loaded from
a URL), an icon is a *word* the renderer maps onto its platform's native icon
set:

| Renderer | Icon set | Mechanism |
|----------|----------|-----------|
| GTK / desktop | Adwaita (freedesktop) | `GtkImage` + icon-theme name (`…-symbolic`), CSS-tinted |
| Browser / SSR | Lucide | inline `<svg>` (`stroke="currentColor"`), single-sourced |
| macOS / iOS (future) | SF Symbols | `Image(systemName:)` |

The **application owns the intent** (the neutral name); the **renderer owns the
visual** (which glyph, its default size, its weighting). This mirrors the design
tokens' split (spec/TOKENS.md).

## Protocol

- **Component**: `ICON` `0x0B` (leaf).
- **Property**: `ICON_NAME` `0x1038` (`STRING`, arena ref) — the canonical name.
- Reuses: `LABEL` (accessibility — a presentable icon is `role="img"` +
  `aria-label`; without one the icon is decorative/`aria-hidden`), `COLOR` /
  `foregroundStyle` (tint — Lucide strokes `currentColor`, GTK symbolic icons
  recolor via CSS), `FONT_SIZE` (size — text-style symbol sizing; the renderer
  defaults to its own icon size when absent), and the frame/opacity modifiers.
- `ICON` is a leaf like `IMAGE` — no new events, no children.

## Canonical vocabulary

`ICON_NAME` values are the *protocol contract*: any renderer MUST understand
them. The canonical catalog (48 + 1 icons) lives in `lib/rust/crates/pathland-icons`
— the single source its GTK name + Lucide markup are derived from, and the
`generated/icons.ts` the DOM client consumes. An app may reference a name the
catalog does not yet map; renderers fall back gracefully (GTK `image-missing`,
web an empty-slot glyph) and the catalog can grow by adding one row.

| Name | GTK (symbolic) | Lucide | | Name | GTK (symbolic) | Lucide |
|------|----------------|--------|-|------|----------------|--------|
| `home` | `go-home` | `house` | | `play` | `media-playback-start` | `play` |
| `settings` | `preferences-system` | `settings` | | `pause` | `media-playback-pause` | `pause` |
| `search` | `system-search` | `search` | | `stop` | `media-playback-stop` | `square` |
| `menu` | `open-menu` | `menu` | | `skip-back` | `media-skip-backward` | `skip-back` |
| `close` | `window-close` | `x` | | `skip-forward` | `media-skip-forward` | `skip-forward` |
| `cloud` | `weather-overcast` | `cloud` | | `volume` | `audio-volume-high` | `volume-2` |
| `chevron-left/right/up/down` | `go-previous/next/up/down` | `chevron-*` | | `volume-mute` | `audio-volume-muted` | `volume-x` |
| `arrow-left` / `arrow-right` | `go-previous` / `go-next` | `arrow-*` | | `shuffle` | `media-playlist-shuffle` | `shuffle` |
| `add` | `list-add` | `plus` | | `repeat` | `media-playlist-repeat` | `repeat` |
| `remove` | `list-remove` | `minus` | | `info` | `dialog-information` | `info` |
| `check` | `object-select` | `check` | | `warning` | `dialog-warning` | `alert-triangle` |
| `edit` | `document-edit` | `pencil` | | `error` | `dialog-error` | `alert-circle` |
| `delete` | `edit-delete` | `trash-2` | | `success` | `emblem-ok` | `check-circle` |
| `save` | `document-save` | `save` | | `heart` | `emblem-favorite` | `heart` |
| `share` | `emblem-shared` | `share-2` | | `star` | `non-starred` | `star` |
| `download` | `folder-download` | `download` | | `user` / `users` | `avatar-default` / `system-users` | `user` / `users` |
| `upload` | `folder-upload` | `upload` | | `lock` | `changes-prevent` | `lock` |
| `refresh` | `view-refresh` | `refresh-cw` | | `logout` | `system-log-out` | `log-out` |
| `bell` | `preferences-system-notifications` | `bell` | | `image` | `image-x-generic` | `image` |
| `folder` | `folder` | `folder` | | `music` | `audio-x-generic` | `music` |
| `file` | `text-x-generic` | `file` | | `grid` | `view-grid` | `grid-3x3` |
| `list` | `view-list` | `list` | | `filter` | `view-filter` | `filter` |

The GTK column shows the icon-theme name; renderers append the `-symbolic`
suffix. Where no native GTK glyph exists the freedesktop fallback policy applies
(`image-missing`).

## Semantics

- **Authoring**: `Icon.of(IconName.PLAY)` / `Icon.of("play")` (a canonical
  string, or an app-extension name), `Label.of(title, Icon)`,
  `Button.of(Icon.of(…) , action)`.
- **Size / tint**: `FONT_SIZE` / `COLOR` as on text. Sized like a symbol
  (`1em`, `set_pixel_size`); tinted via `currentColor` / CSS color.
- **Reactivity**: the name is a single `Signal<String>` — a change re-emits only
  the node's `ICON_NAME` delta.
- **Accessibility**: `LABEL` → presentable (`role="img"`, GTK accessible label);
  none → decorative (`aria-hidden`, GTK no accessible label).

## Adding an icon

1. Add the Lucide SVG + a GTK name to `pathland-icons::CATALOG` (one row).
2. Add the `IconName` variant in the Java and Rust DSLs (canonical value).
3. Regenerate `lib/typescript/src/generated/icons.ts` (`npm run regen`).
4. Test: `cargo test -p pathland-icons` (every row resolves everywhere).


## README

 lucide-static-svg 
 
 
 
 An offline Rust crate containing the Lucide icon catalog as generated, embedded SVG data and optional SVG path data. 
 The catalog is generated from official Lucide release archives. Runtime use has no network dependency. 
 Install 
 Add the dependency from crates.io: 
 cargo add lucide-static-svg
 
 Or add it manually to Cargo.toml: 
 [dependencies]
lucide-static-svg = "1"
 
 The svg feature is enabled by default. Enable path-data when raw path geometry is needed: 
 [dependencies]
lucide-static-svg = { version = "1", default-features = false, features = ["svg", "path-data"] }
 
 Alternatively, you can depend on the repository directly via Git: 
 [dependencies]
lucide-static-svg = { git = "https://github.com/scottcg/lucide-svg-static" }
 
 Usage 
 use lucide_static_svg::Icon;

let icon = Icon::ChevronRight;

assert_eq!(icon.name(), "chevron-right");
assert_eq!(icon.asset_path(), "assets/lucide/chevron-right.svg");

#[cfg(feature = "svg")]
let svg = icon.svg_str();

#[cfg(feature = "path-data")]
let paths = icon.path_data();
 
 Icon also provides all(), from_asset_path(), view_box(), and Display support. The crate exports the embedded Lucide version and source metadata as LUCIDE_VERSION, LUCIDE_RELEASE_TAG, LUCIDE_ICON_COUNT, and LUCIDE_SOURCE_URL. 
 Features 
 
 
 
 Feature 
 Default 
 Provides 
 
 
 
 
 svg 
 Yes 
 Embedded SVG strings and byte slices 
 
 
 path-data 
 No 
 SVG path geometry 
 
 
 
 Development 
 The workspace contains the catalog crate and an xtask generator. To regenerate the catalog from a local Lucide release archive: 
 cargo run -p xtask -- generate \
 --archive /path/to/lucide-icons-<version>.zip \
 --output crates/lucide-static-svg/src/generated \
 --tag <version>
 
 For an extracted icon directory, use --input <directory> instead of --archive. 
 Before submitting changes, run: 
 cargo fmt --all -- --check
cargo check --workspace
cargo test --workspace --all-features
cargo clippy --workspace --all-features --all-targets -- -D warnings
 
 Release workflow 
.github/workflows/lucide-release.yml runs weekly and can also be started manually with an optional Lucide version. It: 
 
 Downloads and verifies the official Lucide release archive. 
 Regenerates the catalog when a release is needed. 
 Runs formatting, checks, tests, and Clippy. 
 Packages and publishes the crate to crates.io. 
 Commits generated changes and creates or refreshes a GitHub release containing the.crate artifact.

Given the plan-mode context, let me step back and think about what the plan should be. The key finding: **Lucide has no official filled set**; filled versions exist only via the unofficial `lucide-extended` (React package, `icons.json` + dist). 

So the real decision for the user is *where the filled data comes from*, since there's no drop-in official source:

**Option 1 — Vendored filled glyphs from `lucide-extended` (unofficial).**
- Source: `lucide-extended-react` 0.2.0 (ISC, V 0.2.0, 6 days ago; 1,387 filled). It has `icons.json` (metadata: which names have `filled`) and `dist/` containing the filled SVG node arrays (paths incl. `<defs><mask>` for holes, matching the doc's approach).
- Extraction: a script reads the dist module(s), extracts each `<Filled>` icon's path data (the "filled" variant array), maps name→inner SVG markup, and emits into our catalog data (Rust static or a generated TS/Rust file). Then `pathland-icons` uses the filled markup.
- Risk: unofficial, updates can change; the dist is React arrays needing transformation to plain SVG (some icons use masks/defs for "holes" — triangle-alert uses a mask to punch the `!`; play/pause likely filled polygons).
- Quality: filled Lucide variants look good (that's the point).

**Option 2 — Author filled SVG data ourselves for the curated 49.**
- I hand-author filled paths per canonical icon. Full control, no new dependency, but error-prone/ugly for complex icons (settings gear, user). High effort, quality risk.

**Option 3 — Keep Lucide stroke icons but render as filled via `fill="currentColor"` + `stroke-width=0`.**
- Only works for closed-shape icons; known-broken for open-line icons (menu, chevron, search handle, plus/minus). NOT recommended as a blanket change. But could apply per-icon where it works... inconsistent, and many of our icons won't fill correctly.

**Option 4 — Use a different official filled icon set for the browser** (e.g., Material Symbols rounded/filled, Bootstrap Icons filled) while mapping names to it. But user said Lucide. Could ask.

Given the user's clear directive ("the lucide icons used in the browser should be the filled ones"), Option 1 is the best fit: genuinely filled Lucide icons, single-sourced, reusable across HTML+TS. The extraction is mechanical from the unofficial package.

But there's a real subtlety: the `icons.json` I fetched references component names but no SVG data. The dist is 2.34MB of React component arrays. # pathland-icons — implementation status

**Last updated:** October 6, 2026

The canonical icon catalog for the `ICON` primitive (spec/ICONS.md): a curated
set of neutral semantic names, single-sourced with their per-renderer native
mappings.

## Implemented

- **Catalog** (`CATALOG`): 49 entries, each `Icon(name, gtk, remix_id, web_inner)`.
- **GTK mapping** (`gtk_icon_name`): Adwaita/freedesktop **symbolic** icon-theme
  names.
- **Remix Icon (filled) web data** (`remix_id` / `web_inner` / `WEB_SVG_OPEN` /
  `WEB_SVG_CLOSE`): **filled** single-`<path>` inner SVG markup vendored from
  Remix Icon v4.9.1 (Apache-2.0 — see `THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md`); the shell uses
  `fill="currentColor"` so `COLOR` tints the glyph. Consumed by
  `pathland-render-html` (SSR) and `pathland-ts-codegen` (→ the DOM client's
  `generated/icons.ts`).
- **Lookup + fallbacks**: `lookup` / `is_canonical` / `gtk_fallback`
  (`image-missing`) / `web_fallback_svg` for app-authored names the catalog
  does not map.
- **`no_std`** const data only (no `alloc`).

## Not implemented / gaps

- Only 49 curated icons; extending = add a catalog row (+ a Remix `-fill` glyph
  + a GTK name) and regenerate — the mechanism is the point, not the breadth.
- GTK names are best-effort theme lookups; an unavailable name falls back to the
  icon theme's `image-missing`, never a broken render.

## Verified by

`cargo test -p pathland-icons` — every catalog entry resolves on every renderer,
canonical names are unique, unknown names resolve to fallbacks.

# Icons — the `ICON` primitive and canonical vocabulary

The `ICON` primitive (0x0B) renders a **renderer-native symbol** for a canonical,
semantic name written once in the UI model. Unlike `IMAGE` (an asset loaded from
a URL), an icon is a *word* the renderer maps onto its platform's native icon
set:

| Renderer | Icon set | Mechanism |
|----------|----------|-----------|
| GTK / desktop | Adwaita (freedesktop) | `GtkImage` + icon-theme name (`…-symbolic`), CSS-tinted |
| Browser / SSR | **Remix Icon, filled** | inline `<svg>` (`fill="currentColor"`), single-sourced |
| macOS / iOS (future) | SF Symbols | `Image(systemName:)` |

The **application owns the intent** (the neutral name); the **renderer owns the
visual** (which glyph, its default size, its weighting). This mirrors the design
tokens' split (spec/TOKENS.md).

## Protocol

- **Component**: `ICON` `0x0B` (leaf).
- **Property**: `ICON_NAME` `0x1038` (`STRING`, arena ref) — the canonical name.
- Reuses: `LABEL` (accessibility — a presentable icon is `role="img"` +
  `aria-label`; without one the icon is decorative/`aria-hidden`), `COLOR` /
  `foregroundStyle` (tint — the web glyph fills `currentColor`, GTK symbolic
  icons recolor via CSS), `FONT_SIZE` (size — text-style symbol sizing; the
  renderer defaults to its own icon size when absent), and the frame/opacity
  modifiers.
- `ICON` is a leaf like `IMAGE` — no new events, no children.

## Canonical vocabulary

`ICON_NAME` values are the *protocol contract*: any renderer MUST understand
them. The canonical catalog (49 icons) lives in `lib/rust/crates/pathland-icons`
— the single source its GTK name + filled web markup are derived from, and the
`generated/icons.ts` the DOM client consumes. An app may reference a name the
catalog does not yet map; renderers fall back gracefully (GTK `image-missing`,
web an empty-slot glyph) and the catalog can grow by adding one row.

The **web glyphs are the filled variants of the Remix Icon set** (every icon
exists as both `-line` and `-fill`; we vendor the `-fill`). The GTK column shows
the icon-theme name; renderers append the `-symbolic` suffix. Where no native
GTK glyph exists the freedesktop fallback policy applies (`image-missing`).

| Name | GTK (symbolic) | Remix (filled) | Name | GTK (symbolic) | Remix (filled) |
|------|----------------|----------------|------|----------------|----------------|

## Semantics

- **Authoring**: `Icon.of(IconName.PLAY)` / `Icon.of("play")` (a canonical
  string, or an app-extension name), `Label.of(title, Icon)`,
  `Button.of(Icon.of(…) , action)`.
- **Size / tint**: `FONT_SIZE` / `COLOR` as on text. Sized like a symbol
  (`1em`, `set_pixel_size`); tinted via `currentColor` / CSS color. The web
  glyph is **filled** — `fill="currentColor"` on the `<svg>` shell, no stroke.
- **Reactivity**: the name is a single `Signal<String>` — a change re-emits only
  the node's `ICON_NAME` delta.
- **Accessibility**: `LABEL` → presentable (`role="img"`, GTK accessible label);
  none → decorative (`aria-hidden`, GTK no accessible label).

## Adding an icon

1. Pick the Remix `-fill` glyph + a GTK name; add one row to
   `pathland-icons::CATALOG`.
2. Add the `IconName` variant in the Java and Rust DSLs (canonical value).
3. Regenerate `lib/typescript/src/generated/icons.ts` (`npm run regen`).
4. Test: `cargo test -p pathland-icons` (every row resolves everywhere).

# Icons — the `ICON` primitive and canonical vocabulary

The `ICON` primitive (0x0B) renders a **renderer-native symbol** for a canonical,
semantic name written once in the UI model. Unlike `IMAGE` (an asset loaded from
a URL), an icon is a *word* the renderer maps onto its platform's native icon
set.

> **The spec is the vocabulary contract only.** It lists the icons that are
> spec'ed — the `ICON_NAME` values every renderer MUST understand. **Which
> native glyph each renderer draws for a name is renderer-owned** (like
> design-token *values*): Adwaita on GTK, the filled Remix set on the web, SF
> Symbols on Apple. The mapping never appears in the spec; each renderer
> defines its own.

The **application owns the intent** (the neutral name); the **renderer owns the
visual** (which glyph, its default size, its weighting). This mirrors the design
tokens' split (spec/TOKENS.md).

## Protocol

- **Component**: `ICON` `0x0B` (leaf).
- **Property**: `ICON_NAME` `0x1038` (`STRING`, arena ref) — the canonical name.
- Reuses: `LABEL` (accessibility — a presentable icon is `role="img"` +
  `aria-label`; without one the icon is decorative/`aria-hidden`), `COLOR` /
  `foregroundStyle` (tint — the glyph fills/strokes `currentColor`; GTK symbolic
  icons recolor via CSS), `FONT_SIZE` (size — text-style symbol sizing; the
  renderer defaults to its own icon size when absent), and the frame/opacity
  modifiers.
- `ICON` is a leaf like `IMAGE` — no new events, no children.

## Canonical vocabulary

`ICON_NAME` values are the *protocol contract*. The canonical names live in
`pathland_core::constants::icon` (the single protocol-authoritative list every
renderer and DSL binds to). An app may reference a name the vocabulary does not
(yet) contain; renderers fall back gracefully (GTK `image-missing`, web an
empty-slot glyph) and the vocabulary can grow.

| Name | Name | Name | Name |
|------|------|------|------|
| `home` | `settings` | `search` | `menu` |
| `close` | `cloud` | `chevron-left` | `chevron-right` |
| `chevron-up` | `chevron-down` | `arrow-left` | `arrow-right` |
| `add` | `remove` | `check` | `edit` |
| `delete` | `save` | `share` | `download` |

## Semantics

- **Authoring**: `Icon.of(IconName.PLAY)` / `Icon.of("play")` (a canonical
  string, or an app-extension name), `Label.of(title, Icon)`,
  `Button.of(Icon.of(…) , action)`.
- **Size / tint**: `FONT_SIZE` / `COLOR` as on text. Sized like a symbol
  (`1em`, `set_pixel_size`); tinted via `currentColor` / CSS color.
- **Reactivity**: the name is a single `Signal<String>` — a change re-emits only
  the node's `ICON_NAME` delta.
- **Accessibility**: `LABEL` → presentable (`role="img"`, GTK accessible label);
  none → decorative (`aria-hidden`, GTK no accessible label).

## Adding an icon

1. Add the name to `spec/ICONS.md` + `pathland_core::constants::icon` (the
   protocol vocabulary).
2. Add the `IconName` variant in the Java and Rust DSLs (canonical value — the
   Rust variant binds `pathland_core::icon::…`).
3. Each renderer adds its **own** glyph for the name:
   `pathland-render-gtk` (its `gtk_icon_name` map), `pathland-render-html`
   (`icons.rs` — the web owner of the filled glyph). Regenerate
   `lib/typescript/src/generated/icons.ts` (`npm run regen`).
4. Test: `cargo test` (core vocabulary, each renderer's map covers the
   vocabulary).

# Icons — the `ICON` primitive and canonical vocabulary

The `ICON` primitive (0x0B) renders a **renderer-native symbol** for a canonical,
semantic name written once in the UI model. Unlike `IMAGE` (an asset loaded from
a URL), an icon is a *word* the renderer maps onto its platform's native icon
set.

> **The spec is the vocabulary contract only.** It lists the icons that are
> spec'ed — the `ICON_NAME` values every renderer MUST understand. **Which
> native glyph each renderer draws for a name is renderer-owned** (like the
> concrete values of design tokens): the mapping never appears in the spec;
> each renderer defines its own.

The **application owns the intent** (the neutral name); the **renderer owns the
visual** (which glyph, its default size, its weighting). This mirrors the design
tokens' split (spec/TOKENS.md).

## Protocol

- **Component**: `ICON` `0x0B` (leaf).
- **Property**: `ICON_NAME` `0x1038` (`STRING`, arena ref) — the canonical name.
- Reuses: `LABEL` (accessibility — a `LABEL` makes the icon presentable, absent
  makes it decorative), `COLOR` / `foregroundStyle` (tint), `FONT_SIZE` (size —
  text-style symbol sizing; the renderer owns its default size when absent), and
  the frame/opacity modifiers.
- `ICON` is a leaf like `IMAGE` — no new events, no children.

## Canonical vocabulary

`ICON_NAME` values are the *protocol contract*. The canonical names live in
`pathland_core::constants::icon` (`NAMES`, `is_canonical`) — the single
protocol-authoritative list every renderer and DSL binds to. An app may
reference a name the vocabulary does not (yet) contain; renderers fall back
however they own the mapping does, and the vocabulary can grow.

- **Navigation**: `home` `search` `menu` `close` `chevron-left` `chevron-right`
  `chevron-up` `chevron-down` `arrow-left` `arrow-right`
- **Actions**: `add` `remove` `check` `edit` `delete` `save` `share` `download`
  `upload` `refresh` `lock` `logout`
- **Media**: `play` `pause` `stop` `skip-back` `skip-forward` `volume`
  `volume-mute` `shuffle` `repeat` `music`
- **Status**: `info` `warning` `error` `success` `heart` `star` `bell` `cloud`
- **People**: `user` `users`
- **System**: `settings` `grid` `list` `filter`
- **Content**: `folder` `file` `image`

## Semantics

- **Authoring**: `Icon.of(IconName.PLAY)` / `Icon.of("play")` (a canonical
  string, or an app-extension name), `Label.of(title, Icon)`,
  `Button.of(Icon.of(…) , action)`.
- **Size / tint**: `FONT_SIZE` / `COLOR` as on text. Sized like a symbol (the
  renderer owns its default size); tinted for the active scheme.
- **Reactivity**: the name is a single `Signal<String>` — a change re-emits only
  the node's `ICON_NAME` delta.
- **Accessibility**: `LABEL` makes the icon presentable; without one the icon is
  decorative (not announced, not interactive).

## Adding an icon

1. Add the name to `spec/ICONS.md` + `pathland_core::constants::icon` (the
   protocol vocabulary).
2. Add the `IconName` variant in the Java and Rust DSLs (canonical value — the
   Rust variant binds `pathland_core::icon::…`).
3. Each renderer adds its **own** glyph for the name (renderer-owned mapping).
4. Test: the core vocabulary is canonical + unique, and every renderer covers
   the vocabulary.

**Reserved framework root** — the host reserves **`/_pathland/**`** for its own
system endpoints, so app routes never collide with them: the WebSocket lives at
`/_pathland/ws`, the DOM-client bundle at `/_pathland/dom-renderer.js`, the
renderer-owned icon glyphs at `/_pathland/icons/<name>.svg` (served from the

did not embed), and the host's asset mount at `/_pathland/assets/**`. App routes
are everything else (served by the SSR catch-all). The DOM client reads the
base from the SSR page's `data-pathland-base` attribute (default `/_pathland`),
so a host can relocate it behind a proxy. Asset references in the UI model are
**absolute** (`/_pathland/assets/icons/home.svg`) so deep-linked routes resolve
correctly.

# pathland-ts-codegen — implementation status

**Last updated:** September 25, 2026

Generates the TypeScript DOM renderer's protocol-derived files from the canonical
Rust sources, so the TS side cannot drift silently.

## Implemented

- **`constants.ts`** (`lib/typescript/src/constants.ts`): every wire constant is
  bound to its `pathland_core::constants` source (a rename breaks compilation, a
  revalue changes the emitted file); the protocol-semantic enum codes (alignment,
  shape kind, state, …) are enumerated from `spec/` — `ROLE_*` is bound to
  `pathland_core::constants::role` (the semantic-only catalog, dense 0–13) and
  `TEXT_STYLE_*` to `pathland_core::constants::text_style`.
- **`generated/tokens-core.ts`** (`lib/typescript/src/generated/tokens-core.ts`):
  the design-token conventions (`tokenToCssVar`, `isDarkToken`,
  `isLengthToken`, `resolveTokenCssRef` + length-token tables) emitted from
  `pathland_render_html::token_spec` — the single source the Rust renderer and
  the DOM client share. `src/tokens.ts` imports it.
- **`generated/role-spec.ts`** (`lib/typescript/src/generated/role-spec.ts`):
  the semantic `ROLE` → element + typography → heading conventions emitted from
  `pathland_render_html::role_spec` — `ROLE_TAGS`, `HEADING_STYLES`,
  `ShellKind`, and the `semanticTag`/`textTag`/`ariaRole`/`headingLevel`
  resolvers — so semantic-tag / ARIA / heading decisions cannot drift between
  the Rust SSR renderer and the DOM client. `constants.ts` also carries the
  media surface (`COMPONENT_AUDIO`/`VIDEO`, `PROP_AUDIO_SOURCE`/`VIDEO_SOURCE`)
  and the icon surface (`COMPONENT_ICON`, `PROP_ICON_NAME`).
- **`generated/icons.ts`** (`lib/typescript/src/generated/icons.ts`): the
  canonical icon catalog mirrored from `pathland-render-html::icons` — `ICONS` (canonical
  `ICON_NAME` → Remix **filled** inner SVG markup) plus the SVG shell +
  fallback strings —
  so the DOM client renders exactly what the Rust SSR renderer emits and the two
  cannot drift.
- **`npm run regen`** (`lib/typescript/scripts/regen.mjs`) runs both generators
  (and the golden-fixture emitter); CI's `rust` job runs them and fails on
  `git diff --exit-code` drift.

## Regenerate

`npm run regen` (from `lib/typescript`) or `cargo run -p pathland-ts-codegen`
(from `lib/rust`), then commit the generated files with the change that produced
them.

## Not implemented / gaps

- Only the pure-data surfaces are generated. The element-shell factory
  (`elements.ts`) and the property-handler table (`classes.ts`) are still
  hand-written — their alignment is enforced behaviorally by the
  `pathland-html-golden` conformance harness rather than generated. Extending
  the generator to those tables is the planned next step.

# pathland-render-html (Java) — implementation status

**Last updated:** October 2, 2026

The **Java binding to the Rust HTML renderer** (`com.pathland.render.html`) — a
thin **JNA shim** over `libpathland_render_html`. There is a **single renderer**
(the Rust crate), reused by every language; the former hand-written retained
Java renderer is removed. Protocol contract: `spec/`.

## Implemented

- **Stateless JNA shim**: `HtmlRenderer.instance()` links the Rust cdylib;
  `render(frame, root)` / `renderFragment(frame, root)` /
  `renderFullSnapshot(frame, root)` render a self-contained snapshot frame to
  HTML in one pass (no retained tree, no `applyFrame`); `pathland_html_free`
  releases native strings. Lazy-loaded; skipped (test assumption) when the dylib
  is absent from `java.library.path`.
- **Debug comments**: `renderDebug(frame, root)` / `renderFragmentDebug(...)`
  bind the Rust `pathland_html_render_debug` exports — each rendered node is
  prefixed with an HTML comment naming its component type and the modifiers
  applied (opt-in; the plain `render` output is unchanged).
- **Full Rust renderer surface** (canonical): all spec components render inline
  (structural + decorative CSS in a single `style` attribute), ARIA/event
  attributes, `IS_SECURE` → password, `TOGGLE_STYLE` variants,
  `DATE_PICKER_MODE`, and literal colors inline. The renderer injects its own
  built-in `<style>` block (preflight reset + design tokens + `.pathland-*`
  component defaults) into every document — no external CSS, no `/tailwind.css`.
- **Demos use the shim**: `SessionApp` no longer calls `applyFrame`; SSR renders
  the mount frame through `HtmlRenderer.render(sink.frame(), rootId)`. The
  renderer is compiled once at startup.
- **Text fields share one component class**: `TEXT_FIELD` inputs and `TEXT_EDITOR`
  textareas render with `class="pathland-input"` (Tailwind-style inset-outline
  styling from the Rust renderer's CSS); the copied `@pathland/dom-renderer`
  bundle mirrors the class so delta-created fields hydrate identically.

## Removed (September 2026)

- `compileTailwind(overrideCss)` and the `pathland_tailwind_compile` binding are
  **deleted** — the renderer is inline-only now and needs no compiler. The demo
  `/tailwind.css` endpoints (`TailwindCssController` / `TailwindCssResource`)
  and the `<link rel="stylesheet" href="/tailwind.css">` in both `SessionApp`

  accessibility label, `ContentMode Fill`→`cover`).

is absent); part of the non-demo reactor run on JDK 17.

Fixed. The play/pause icon failing to change was a **client-side self-match bug** in the lazy resolver (not the emitter or server):

## Root cause
`setIcon` rewrote the element's `data-pathland-icon` to the new name **before** scanning for an embedded glyph — and that scan includes the element itself. So on the play→pause delta, the button svg suddenly "matched" its own new attr and pasted back its **old play glyph** → the icon never changed (no fetch, no error). A freshly created in-document icon also self-copied empty content.

## Fix (`lib/typescript/src/icons.ts`)
`setIcon` now **resolves before mutating** — the memo/embedded-glyph lookup runs against the truthful pre-mutation DOM (the button still advertises `play`), so `pause` falls through to the fallback + lazy fetch of `/_pathland/icons/pause.svg`. SSR-parity attr assignment stays on the success paths.

## Regression coverage (+3 tests, 206 total pass)
- `icons.test.ts`: **same-element toggle on a hydrated svg** (play→pause→play), asserting it never pastes its own glyph; fresh in-document icon never left blank.
- `apply.test.ts`: a real `PROP_ICON_NAME=pause` **delta over a hydrated play button** — the live WS path.

- Both demos serve glyphs: Spring (`/_pathland/icons/play|pause.svg` → 200, `image/svg+xml`, `immutable`) and Quarkus (global **and** mounted `/app2` base — RESTEasy falls through, no shadowing).

The user observes: click play → loads & shows pause (one fetch). Click play again → loads & shows play. They ask: why does the play icon LOAD? Isn't it embedded from the start?

Their observation is correct and matches my design. The reason play ALSO loads:

The SSR embeds the play glyph inline in the hydrated page (initial state). So play IS embedded at the start — but only as **raw DOM content**, NOT in the client's JS memo `cache`. When the user clicks play twice:
1. Initial: button svg `data-pathland-icon="play"` + play glyph inline (from SSR). 
2. Click → playing=true → delta ICON_NAME=pause → `setIcon(button, "pause")`: cache miss for pause, embeddedGlyph("pause") → no other pause svg → miss → FALLBACK + **fetch pause.svg** → caches pause → shows pause.
3. Click again → playing=false → delta ICON_NAME=play → `setIcon(button, "play")`: cache.get("play") → MISS (play was never fetched — it was only embedded as the element's own initial inline content, which is NOT the client memo). embeddedGlyph("play") → scans the document for a `[data-pathland-icon="play"]` svg → the only play svg was the button, and it now advertises "pause" (after step 2's attr rewrite) → miss → FALLBACK + **fetch play.svg** → caches → shows play.

So play "loads" because (a) the embedded-copy mechanism keyed on the element's `data-pathland-icon` attr only finds the element when it advertises "play" — after the first toggle it advertises "pause", and (b) play was never memoized because memoization only happens through the fetch path (the initial SSR embed doesn't write to the JS cache).

So the "embedded from the start" glyph is single-use: it seeds the display, but on the FIRST toggle the element's attr flips to pause, and the play glyph "evaporates" from the seeded pool — so the return trip needs a fetch.

The user is essentially asking: can we avoid re-fetching play? The answer: yes — we can **memoize the embedded seed**. When `setIcon` finds a glyph via `embeddedGlyph`, also write it into `cache` so future swaps to that name are instant. Then:

- Initial state is embedded (not in cache). First toggle to pause: pause fetched (unavoidable — element only ever showed play; no pause glyph exists anywhere in the page). Cached.
- Toggle back to play: cache now... would play be cached? Under "seed the cache on embedded hit": the FIRST time we ever RESOLVED play via embedded, we'd cache it. But we never resolve play until the user toggles back — at that point the button advertises "pause", so embeddedGlyph("play") misses, cache misses → fetch. To cache play's embedded glyph, we'd need to seed it at the start (during hydration / initial ICON_NAME apply) — i.e., when the element FIRST shows play (from SSR), the client doesn't run setIcon at boot (no delta). So play never enters the cache unless we explicitly harvest embedded seeds at boot or on first use.

Better fixes:

**Option A — memoize on embedded hit (partial).** When `embeddedGlyph` returns a glyph, also `cache.set(name, glyph)`. Effect on the play/pause loop: First pause toggle: pause not embedded → fetch+cache pause. Back to play: play not in cache (never seen a play embedded hit), and no embedded play remains → fetch play+cache. So both still fetched once. No improvement for THIS case.

**Option B — capture each element's own seed as it's superseded.** When toggling pause, BEFORE overwriting the element, the old embedded glyph (play) could be harvested into the cache (the element is being changed away from play → its content is a valid play glyph → memoize it). Then toggling back to play = instant cache hit. This eliminates the play re-fetch: every swap captures the previous glyph into the memo. Elegant and cheap: in setIcon, when resolving a swap that will REPLACE an element currently showing name `old`, stash `svg.dataset`-driven old glyph into cache under the old name.

Actually simpler framing: on each setIcon, the element currently advertises `data-pathland-icon=old` (or none) with old's glyph. Before we replace it, we can memoize `cache.set(old, svg.innerHTML)` (if old non-empty and content non-empty). Then:
- t0: button play (embedded). 
- t1 → pause: old="play", cache.set("play", playGlyph) [harvest], then set pause (fetch once, cache).
- t2 → play: cache hit play → instant, no fetch.
- t3 → pause: cache hit pause → instant. 

So the ONLY fetch ever is the very first transition to the never-before-shown icon. After one round, every toggle is purely local. This directly addresses "why does play load" — after the change, neither loads after the first round.

**Option C — seed the cache from the whole hydrated DOM at boot** (harvest all embedded `[data-pathland-icon]` siblings into the memo as the page hydrates). This is the "SSR is the preload" idea made explicit in cache form: at boot, iterate `svg.pathland-icon[data-pathland-icon]`, and for each dedupe `cache.set(name, innerHTML)`. Then the FIRST toggle to pause still fetches (pause never embedded), but any *revisit* to a name that was ever embedded (including the original play, and any icon elsewhere in the page like skip-back/skip-forward/volume) is instant. That also handles the case where multiple icons of the same name exist (dedupe).

Wait — but harvesting at boot is basically what `embeddedGlyph` does lazily, except lazy harvest misses the "superseded" case (element no longer advertises the old name). Actually no: at boot, play IS advertised → cache seeded with play. Then:
- t1 → pause: cache(play)=hit? No — cache(play) was seeded at boot, but we're calling setIcon(button,"pause"); pause miss + not embedded → fetch pause.
- t2 → play: cache(play) seeded at boot → INSTANT. No fetch. ✓
- t3 → pause: cache(pause) hit → instant.

So Option C alone (boot-time seed of all embedded glyphs) fully solves the play re-fetch: play was seeded at boot into the cache. pause is fetched once on first toggle. This is clean and robust — and semantically matches the user's mental model ("isn't play embedded from the start" → yes, so memorize it from the start).

Note: The DOM-seed path (embeddedGlyph) already exists for the case where the OTHER name is currently shown elsewhere. Boot-seeding the cache generalizes it and also covers the same-name revisit after the element changed.

Also note: my boot isn't the only entry — the client might apply the initial snapshot only once. Where would boot-harvest go? In `index.ts` boot (after hydration, before/after connecting), or lazily: on `setIcon` miss we could ALSO seed every currently-embedded glyph into the cache (harvest all at first icon swap). That's cheaper than a dedicated boot pass and avoids extra work on static pages that never toggle icons. I.e., when a swap MISSES (cache+embedded), harvest ALL embedded glyphs into the cache (one querySelectorAll pass) before deciding; then re-check. That way:
- t1 → pause: miss → harvest {play: glyphINCACHE} (from the button + any others) → pause still not found → fetch pause.
- t2 → play: cache(play) hit → instant.

Harvest-on-first-miss is the pragmatic version (no boot cost; only pages that toggle icons pay one query pass). And it retains correctness for the later case.

Great question — your intuition is right, and the reason it fetches is a one-time gap in my memoization. Here's what happens:

## Why "play" loads after "pause"

Play **is** embedded from the start — but only as **DOM content**, never entered into the client's JS memo:

1. SSR shows the button svg `data-pathland-icon="play"` + the play `<path>` inline.
2. Click → delta `pause` → `setIcon`: pause is in no cache, appears nowhere in the DOM → **fetch pause.svg** (memoized after).
3. Click → delta `play` → `setIcon`: `cache.get("play")` is **a miss** (play was never *fetched* — its embedded copy was DOM-only), and the only play svg was the button, which now advertises `pause` → no embedded play remains → **fetch play.svg**.

So the embedded seed is "single-use": the instant the element flips to pause, play stops being discoverable anywhere. Each side loads exactly once (then both are memoized), but the return trip to play can be made instant.

## Fix — harvest embedded glyphs into the memo on first miss

Add a small `harvestEmbedded()` in `icons.ts`: on a `setIcon` miss, scan the document's `svg.pathland-icon[data-pathland-icon]` once and write each glyph into `cache` (skipping empty content), then re-check. Same behaviour as today, plus:

- t0: button = play (embedded).
- t1 → pause: miss → **harvest saves play's glyph into the cache** → pause still absent → fetch pause (once).

Facts from the code I've read:

**Per-report cost (wire)**: A MEDIA_TIME_UPDATED event is a 16-byte opcode (EVENT category, command 0x10, targetId u32, seconds f32). Over the network it's the PLPL batch encoding (a self-contained batch with header). Each report = one 16-byte opcode in the event ring/batch. So wire bytes per report ≈ 16 B (+ tiny batch framing). At 30 Hz → ~480 B/s per playing audio node. Negligible.

**Web sampler cost**: a `setInterval` at 33 ms with a trivial handler (getter compares, one event encode + WS send when gate passes). Note: reporting is gated on actual playback progress — at 30 Hz actual, you get ~30 events/s. The interval callback on each tick (30/s, even when paused it's a cheap branch; we check `media.paused` first). CPU cost trivial (≤ a few µs per tick; a couple % of one core at absolute worst, typically <<0.1%).

**GTK sampler cost**: the media worker loop is ALREADY a busy-ish loop: `recv_timeout` (blocking up to poll interval) + bus drain (non-blocking `timed_pop(ZERO)`) + `query_position`. Going 250→33 ms means the loop wakes 30×/s instead of 4×/s. `query_position` on a GStreamer playbin each wake (~33ms): GStreamer can cold-cache the running time without a full round-trip (playbin/query_position usually fast, sub-µs to µs). CPU: still negligible overall. The main-thread drain timer at 33ms — GTK main loop timeout handlers are cheap; 30 wakeups/s is trivial. The bash warning: none.

**App-side amplification**: This is the bigger consideration. On the WEB demo, each MEDIA_TIME_UPDATED report goes WS→Java app→ the `onPositionReport(position)` display signal. Negligible — this is one of the cheapest places to spend 30 Hz. Breakdown:

**Wire cost (the only real cost)**
- Each `MEDIA_TIME_UPDATED` is **one 16-byte EVENT opcode** (id + `seconds` f32).

**Web sampler**

**GTK sampler**
- Worker loop `recv_timeout` 250→33 ms: 30 wakeups/s instead of 4, with a **`query_position` on playbin** per wake (~µs-level; GStreamer cheaply reports running time). Main-thread drain timer at 33 ms is 30 no-op timeout callbacks/s. Still sub-1% of one core. Scales linearly per playing node (demo has one).

**Two watch-items (not blockers)**
1. **App-side amplification**: every report flushes the app's position signal → the emitter re-emits only the bound nodes (~1 more opcode each) 30×/s. Fine-grained emission keeps this trivial; only *persisted* state or heavy computed chains would amortize badly — the demo neither persists position nor computes much per report.
2. **Background throttling**: browsers cap background-tab timers to ≥1 s, and GTK timers throttle on an occluded window — so the 30 Hz is best-effort when the app is visible/focused, which is exactly when it matters.

The key concept: a container that picks one of its children based on available space.

**CRITICAL ARCHITECTURAL CONSTRAINT**: Pathland's engine is declarative and does **NOT compute layout**. The renderer computes layout natively. "Renderers are Dumb, Applications are Smart." The engine emits structure + constraint properties; native renderers lay out.

So a `ViewThatFits` that "conditionally shows one of X children based on width" is tricky because:
- WHO decides which child to show? The engine (app) must choose based on... available width. But the engine doesn't know the available width — the renderer does.
- The protocol says: renderers MUST NOT retain app state, and apps are Smart (generate commands). But available space is a RENDERER fact.

There are a few possible designs:

**Design A — Renderer-side selection (like CSS container queries / responsive layout)**: The engine emits all candidate children with `condition=fit-{index}` metadata; the renderer measures its available space and shows the first candidate that fits. This is renderer-driven conditional display. The renderer knows the width natively (GTK widget allocation, CSS container query, DOM media/container queries). The engine emits the candidates + the "fit" property; the renderer picks. This matches "renderer computes layout" well and is highly performant (native pick, no round-trips). But it introduces renderer-side "state"? No — it's a pure function of available size + emitted candidates → which child shows. Renderer retains no business state (the chosen candidate is a layout output, like the rendered-output tree cache). This is the "WHAT versus WHERE" question: selecting among the SAME semantic alternatives is arguably a layout action (WHERE/what-fits), renderer-owned. Actually in SwiftUI, ViewThatFits is a **layout container** — it picks which child to render based on the proposed size, exactly layout. So Pathland's analog = a renderer-side container. That's Design A.

SwiftUI's `ViewThatFits` is a layout container that proposes sizes to its children and picks the first that fits — it's inherently renderer/layout-side, based on the space proposed to it by its parent (not the whole viewport).

So the user wants a `ViewThatFits`/`SizeThatFits` that measures the **available space the parent offers**, per node, natively — not the window width. That means:
- Renderer-side: the container's own allocated size (GTK widget allocation; CSS container query / flex box in web).
- The candidate selection depends on how much space the container actually got, which is layout.

This is Design A (renderer-side fit container) — the SwiftUI-faithful one. The viewport-based B approach is rejected by the user.

Now I need to plan accordingly. Key implications and questions:

**Protocol design (Design A — renderer-led)**
- New component type, e.g., `VIEW_THAT_FITS` (group: Layout & Container 0x10–0x1F; e.g., 0x17/0x1D? — there are gaps: 0x17, 0x18, 0x19, 0x1A are unused within that range; actually 0x13 GRID, 0x14 SCROLLVIEW, 0x15 LAZY_VGRID, 0x16 LAZY_HGRID, 0x1B LAZY_VSTACK, 0x1C LAZY_HSTACK — so 0x17–0x1A are free and 0x1D–0x1F).

Candidate children are numbered 0..N-1 in fit-order (first = most-preferred/easiest-to-fit).
- Renderer behavior: measure the container's available space; evaluate candidates in order; pick the FIRST whose **ideal/intrinsic size fits** within the space (SwiftUI semantics: propose the ideal size; first child that fits wins; if none fit, the last one is shown anyway — SwiftUI shows the smallest sized one / last? Actually ViewThatFits falls back to the first child that fits; if none fit it uses the child that would fit best... SwiftUI: "if none fit, the ideal size of the last child" — effectively shows something rather than nothing; the last child is used as fallback without fitting).
- Rendering: only the chosen child must be shown; the others hidden. But the wire—should the renderer render all children and CSS/GTK-hide the non-selected ones (visibility:hidden/display:none), or render only the chosen one? Important: **renderer statelessness / pure function** requires deterministic mapping opcode→output. If the renderer ALWAYS receives all candidates and applies a "hide losers" property, then the DOM/GTK would contain hidden duplicates. That's fine (like `display:none`), but wasteful and events/ARIA leakage concerns. Alternatively, the renderer picks and PHYSICALLY only materializes the chosen child — but then the renderer must know which one to drop BEFORE mapping... it's still pure (same opcodes + same measured size → same pick). The chosen candidate is output, not state. OK.

The renderer picks on EVERY render based on current measured size + candidate set. Deltas that change candidate content → re-measure → maybe pick changes. Consistent.

**Cross-renderer consistency problem** (the big one I identified): the candidate's ideal size differs per renderer (fonts, platform metrics) → different picks on GTK vs web vs (future). E.g., a wide layout vs narrow layout; on GTK with a larger font the wide candidate might not fit → narrow chosen; on web with smaller font the wide fits → wide chosen. For a cross-platform protocol this means the SAME UI can look different on each renderer at the same container size. Is that acceptable? SwiftUI's answer is one layout engine everywhere; Pathland's answer is native layout everywhere. This divergence is inherent to renderer-owned fit. Mitigations:
  - Define fit strictly: candidate "fits" if its **ideal size ≤ available size** on the chosen axis. Ideal size is renderer-measured (text, images). Font differences → divergence.
  - Provide an OPTIONAL inline `FIT_HINT` sizes per candidate (e.g., approximate ideal width) so renderers that can't measure cheaply (or to reduce divergence) use the hint.
  - Accept divergence as a renderer-characteristic (consistent with "renderers own appearance"); docs note it.

Design A (renderer-side native fit):
- Web: a container that does layout with flex + CSS; to select by fit there must be a measurement pass BEFORE the DOM is stable. ## The model

`ViewThatFits`/`SizeThatFits` is a **layout container, not a structural container** — a key distinction from `Conditional`:
- **All candidates are always children of the node** (the wire/tree describes the full alternative set; no app-side pick, no structural reconcile — so it works identically in the Java and Rust DSLs and adds nothing to the emitter).
- **The renderer picks**, based on the size *it* was allocated by its parent (GTK `size_allocate`; the CSS/JS container size on web). The pick is a pure function of (tree, allocated size) — renderer-owned layout output, consistent with "renders may retain their layout tree; never app state."
- A **new `PARAMETER` property set** tells the renderer how to pick; a **new component id** (`0x17`, free in the reserved 0x17–0x1A layout range) is the container.

## Two candidate designs

| | **A — `ViewThatFits` (SwiftUI-faithful)** | **B — `SizeThatFits` / width-query** |
|---|---|---|
| Rule | first child whose **measured ideal size** fits the container | first child whose declared **width threshold** (e.g. `minWidth`) the container **meets** (a band) |
| Web | needs candidates' ideal sizes → JS `ResizeObserver` + measure (flicker risk) *or* app-supplied ideal hints + CSS `@container` | **pure CSS `@container (min-width/max-width)`** — native layout, zero JS, correct at SSR first paint |
| GTK | `gtk_widget_measure` each child in allocator (native, cheap) | numeric band compare in the allocator (cheaper) |
| Cross-renderer | **diverges**: fonts/platform metrics differ → same px can pick differently on GTK vs web | **deterministic**: app-declared thresholds vs container px → identical picks everywhere |
| Perf | O(candidates) structural change only; measurement on change/resize | O(candidates) structural change only; **zero** steady-state, browser re-evaluates `@container` on its own resize |

**Perf verdict**: **B is the clearest win** — the web path is a pure CSS container-query band (each candidate = one `@container (min-width: tᵢ) and (max-width: tᵢ₊₁)` rule; sorted ascending, last band unbounded — natively exclusive, no measurement, no JS, no round-trip, no reflow feedback), and GTK is a one-time numeric compare in the allocator. A is fully possible but pays measurement + a cross-renderer consistency cost.

Both satisfy "what's possible across renderers": web (SSR + DOM), GTK, and any future renderer get the same contract — only the picker differs, and the spec defines the algorithm (candidate order = priority; last candidate = fallback when nothing fits).

The Java emitter has the exact machinery:
- `RenderResult` already carries routed-input registries (tapActions, textInputs, valueInputs, editingInputs, dateInputs, mediaInputs, navigateActions). A `sizeInputs` (Map<Integer, Consumer<Float>> or WritableSignal refs) fits the established pattern.
- Structural slots (`structuralContent`) reconcile via `Signals.effect(() -> reconcileSlot(node))` — a signal (the selector) read inside `structuralContent.get()` is TRACKED, so when the size signal changes, the effect re-runs `reconcileSlot`, which renders the new content, diffs children, and emits TREE/PROPERTY deltas; identical recompute → zero opcodes. Exactly what `SizeThatFits` needs: the width signal is the selector; candidates are DSL-local; MIN_WIDTH never rides the wire.

So the revised design is fully supported by existing infra. The new protocol surface is minimal:
- Component `SIZE_THAT_FITS` 0x17 (a slot container, FILL-sized, MEASURE-observed).
- Property `MEASURE` (report allocated size changes, e.g. 0x1016): marks the container as size-observed.
- Event `SIZE_CHANGED` (host→guest, e.g. 0x13): `{target, width(f32 B), height(f32 C)}`.

Now let me double-check that the renderer→host→app routing for a NEW report type is modeled somewhere concrete: media reports route via `mediaInputs` + `MediaInput` and server-core dispatches `r.media(...)`; taps route `r.tap(id)`; size would route `r.size(id, w, h)`. So `RenderResult` gains `sizeInputs: Map<Integer, BiConsumer<Float,Float>>` (w,h) or a small record. Server-core PathlandHost/registry: the DOM client's WS input dispatch decodes events → calls the registry's input handlers. There's a per-connection `dispatch` that maps EVENT opcodes to registry methods. Adding SIZE_CHANGED decoding + routing = new branch (like media).

Where to send from the client: index.ts `transport` receives...? Actually the DOM client SENDS events (host→guest direction is client→server over WS). The DOM client already sends `encodeEnvironment(...)`, media events, pointer events. It will send `encodeSizeChanged(target, w, h)` (new encode). GTK sends via its event ring/sink: an `Event::SizeChanged` variant → the shared event ring → host drains → app. render-gtk emits `Event::SizeChanged { target, width, height }` from the allocator when changed.

For the web DOM client measuring: a ResizeObserver on the container element (`[data-pathland-measure]` or the SIZE_THAT_FITS node), reporting after hydration + on change, throttled via rAF. Only for nodes carrying the MEASURE attribute (SSR emits it for size-that-fits nodes).

Now — GTK specifics: the slot container = a GTK container widget (Box) that's FILL-sized; on size-allocate report width when changed (>=1 unit delta). The node's child swaps via TREE deltas already handled by render-gtk incremental reconciliation (id→widget map; child widget replaced). Good.

Web SSR: emit `<div data-pathland-id class="pathland-ftf" data-pathland-measure style="...FILL...">` with the single selected child. On SSR, the app's initial selection = threshold-0 candidate (always valid). Client hydrates → ResizeObserver fires immediately → sends SIZE_CHANGED → app recomputes → if same candidate, reconcile emits ZERO opcodes (no flash!) — wait, only if the width band maps to the same candidate. The constraint reshapes the design cleanly — and the necessary machinery already exists. Here's the revised plan.

## Revised model: app-side selection, only the pick transmitted

- `SizeThatFits` becomes a **structural container** (like `Conditional`): the **candidates live only in the DSL** (their `MIN_WIDTH` thresholds never ride the wire). The app selects using the **container's reported width** and the emitter transmits **exactly one child** through the slot — `TREE` deltas swap it when the width band changes; an unchanged selection emits **zero opcodes**.
- The renderer's job is reduced to: (1) size the container node to its parent's proposal, (2) when its allocated width changes, **report it** (a new host→guest event). Selection, comparison, and emission are all app/engine-side — "applications are Smart."
- **This is the `Conditional` precedent, proven**: `Emitter.reconcileSlot` already re-runs on any signal read inside `structuralContent.get()` and diffs/reconciles (identical recompute → zero opcodes). `SizeThatFits` reuses that verbatim, with the width signal as the selector. `RenderResult` already returns routed-input registries (taps/text/value/media) — a `size` sink slots into the same pattern.

## New protocol surface (minimal)
- `component_type::SIZE_THAT_FITS = 0x17` (slot container; FILL-sized so it has a measurable width).
- `property_id::MEASURE` (0x1016): opt-in "report this node's allocated size" so only fitted containers are measured (no blanket reporting).
- **`event::SIZE_CHANGED` (0x13)**: host→guest, `{targetId, width (B f32), height (C f32)}`.

## Across renderers — yes, uniformly
- **Web**: SSR emits `<div data-pathland-id class="pathland-ftf" data-pathland-measure style="width:100%;align-self:stretch">` + the selected child. The DOM client attaches a **`ResizeObserver`** (rAF-throttled) and sends `SizeChanged` on hydration + on resizes. No candidate measurement; unselected candidates are never mounted.
- **GTK**: the container is a FILL-sized widget; in `size-allocate`, when the width changes ≥1, emit `Event::SizeChanged` through the existing event ring/sink.
- **Future renderers**: same two obligations (fill-size + report width). Selection is platform-independent → **identical picks everywhere** (same logical-point width, same band compare).

## What performs best (given the constraint)
- **Wire**: minimal — one child, always; band-crossings = a subtree `TREE` delta; steady-state (same band, or resizes within a band) = **zero emission**. Signal updates inside the hidden... there are no hidden candidates on the wire.
- **Runtime**: no inert hidden widgets (no `display:none` clutter, no ARIA leakage, smaller DOM/GTK widget tree) — strictly better than renderer-led CSS which hides losers in every renderer.
- **Cost (inherent to the constraint)**: a **round-trip on a band crossing** (report → app → swap) and an **initial reconcile**: on SSR the app doesn't know the width, so it renders the **always-valid (threshold-0) candidate first**; after the first report it swaps if a wider band applies. Same-candidate initial report → zero opcodes. This is the SwiftUI parity tradeoff the constraint forces (SwiftUI's pick is layout-native).

## Implementation plan
1. **Spec-first**: `OPCODE.md` (component 0x17 + `MEASURE` 0x1016 + `SIZE_CHANGED` 0x13, f32 width/height), `PRIMITIVES.md`/`LAYOUT.md` (slot is FILL-sized; pick rule = largest candidate threshold ≤ reported width, threshold-0 default; "only the selected child is transmitted"), `EVENTS.md` (SIZE_CHANGED row + cadence: reported on change, throttled), `CONFORMANCE.md` vectors, `DSL.md` rows (Java + Rust).
2. **Core**: `component_type` + `property_id` + `event` constants (+ tests); Java `Components`/`Properties`/`Events` mirrors; TS constants regen.
3. **Emitter (`com.pathland.view.emit`)**: `SizeThatFits` as a `structuralContent` slot (selector = internal width signal, candidates = DSL-local `Fit.of(view, minWidth)` sorted bands); `RenderResult` gains a `sizeInputs` registry; zero-opcodes guarantee falls out of `reconcileSlot`.
4. **DSLs**: Java `SizeThatFits.of(Fit.of(wide, 720), Fit.any(compact))` (default threshold-0 candidate) + Rust `pathland-view` equivalent — both emit the 0x17 slot + `MEASURE` + one child.
5. **Transport/servers**: `SIZE_CHANGED` encoders on the DOM client (ResizeObserver) and GTK (allocate); decode + route into the app's size sink in the WebSocket/ring hosts (registry `size(id,w,h)` → bound signal), mirroring the media-input route.
6. **render-html**: SSR container shell (+ `data-pathland-measure`); **render-gtk**: allocator report + slot widget. Golden `sizethatfits` fixture + `ssr-conformance` + TS (ResizeObserver report) + GTK + Java DSL tests.
7. **Verify**: cargo per-crate, `npm test`, golden `--check`, `mvn install`, `build:all` + repack demos, then a live check that a window/nav resize re-picks and a same-band resize emits nothing. Update all `status.md`.

"Transmit the fit queries to the renderer so it can do the measurement locally" — the renderer receives the fit thresholds (MIN_WIDTH per candidate... but if only the selected child is transmitted, the renderer can't hold unselected candidates to re-select among). So there's tension between "only selected child transmitted" (prior constraint) and "renderer does measurement locally with the queries."

How to reconcile: The renderer receives the fit QUERY (thresholds, i.e., all candidates' MIN_WIDTHs — just the numbers, not the candidate views) + the CURRENTLY selected candidate's VIEW (only the selected child is transmitted). The renderer measures its width locally; when the width crosses a threshold that maps to a DIFFERENT candidate, it tells the app "new fit index" (fit changed event). The app then mounts/swaps the new candidate's view and transmits it (TREE deltas). So:

- Wire carries: the SIZE_THAT_FITS slot + `FIT_QUERY` (the sorted thresholds list) + the currently selected child's subtree (only it).
- Renderer has: the thresholds (numbers, tiny) + the current width (measured locally, no continuous reports!). It computes the fit locally and only sends a `FIT_CHANGED`/`FIT_PICKED {newIndex}` event when the derived fit index changes (a band crossing).
- App: on FIT_CHANGED → recompute which candidate → reconcileSlot swaps subtree → transmits only the new child.
- Continuous width reports: NONE (renderer decides locally). Even better: no size reports at all; renderer sends only discrete "the fit changed" events.

This is strictly better than the previous plan:
1. No continuous SIZE_CHANGED reports flooding the socket on every resize — the renderer evaluates locally and only emits when the FIT (not the raw size) changes.
2. Transmission stays "only the selected child view" (the full candidate set is never transmitted) but the renderer has the tiny threshold table to keep the pick logic local, low-latency, and immediate (no round trip for deciding; round trip only when the pick actually changes and the new subtree must be fetched/emitted).
3. The app doesn't receive a stream of widths to compare — less app churn; the signal only fires on actual fit transitions; the app's reconcile runs only when the emitted child must change.
4. Cross-renderer: the renderer compares its measured width against app-declared thresholds; identical if the widths are in the same units (logical points vs CSS px) and the renderer applies the same "largest threshold ≤ width" rule. Same determinism.

- Fewer events (only fit transitions + the initial one).
- Renderer owns measurement (it already knows its size in its own layout pass — zero extra work; it was going to size-allocate anyway).

Yes — that's a genuine improvement, and it's compatible with everything you've pinned down. Here's the refined design.

## The hybrid: renderer measures, app transmits

**What the renderer receives**: the fit **query** — the sorted candidate **threshold table** (`[720, 480, 0]`) as a LIST property on the container — plus the **currently selected child** (only ever one child on the wire, as you required).

**What the renderer does**: it already knows its own allocated width from its layout pass (no extra measurement work). It compares that width against the threshold table locally and **only emits one event — `FIT_CHANGED{target, index}` — once after first measure and then whenever the derived fit index actually changes** (a band crossing).

**What the app does**: nothing on ordinary resizes (no inbox traffic); on `FIT_CHANGED` it swaps the DSL-local candidate via the existing structural reconcile — which emits **zero opcodes if the new index maps to the same view**.

## Why it beats reporting the raw size
- **Wire**: resize events (which can be dozens per drag-resize) **never reach the app** — the table is transmitted once, and only discrete fit transitions round-trip. Strictly less traffic than `SIZE_CHANGED` at full width resolution.
- **Latency**: detection is immediate/local; the round-trip happens only when the new subtree must actually be materialized.
- **Constraint honored**: candidate *views* never ride the wire — only the app's single selected child does; the "extra" is the tiny, set-once threshold list.
- **Determinism (unchanged)**: same rule ("largest threshold ≤ measured width", logical points) + same numbers → identical picks on every renderer; candidates remain app-owned.
- **Smaller protocol than the raw-size plan**: we can **drop the `MEASURE` property entirely** (the container is identified by its component type + query present). Renderers need only a local ResizeObserver (web, to *detect* changes, never report size) / a compare in `size-allocate` (GTK).

## New protocol surface (delta)
- `component_type::SIZE_THAT_FITS = 0x17` (FILL-sized slot; unselected children never transmitted).
- `property_id::FIT_QUERY = 0x1016`, value type **`LIST`** — arena-backed `[u32 count][f32 × count]` sorted ascending (stable; equal thresholds → lower index wins). input.newString:
### LazyHStack — `LAZY_HSTACK` 0x1C

Virtualized horizontal stack. **Allocation is identical to `HStack`**; only
realization is windowed.

### SizeThatFits — `SIZE_THAT_FITS` 0x17

A **fit slot**: it shows **one child at a time — the currently selected
candidate — so only that child is ever transmitted**. The app owns the
candidates (their views never ride the wire); it transmits the **fit query**
(`FIT_QUERY`, LIST — the candidates' `minWidth` thresholds, ascending) plus the
selected child. The renderer measures its **own allocated width** (the slot is
size-taking — it stretches to its parent's proposal, never hugs, so it always
has a well-defined width) and selects the fit **locally**:

> **Fit rule** — the selected index is `max{ i : thresholds[i] ≤ measured
> width }` (threshold 0 candidate always qualifies — the fallback); equal
> thresholds pick the **lower index**; before the first measure the app renders
> the threshold-0 candidate (index 0). The measurement is in **logical points**,
> so the pick is identical on every renderer given the same slot width.

The renderer reports its selection back with **`FIT_CHANGED`** ([EVENTS.md](./EVENTS.md))
— emitted **once after the first measure, and then only when the derived fit
index changes** (a band crossing). It never streams the raw size. The app reacts
by swapping the slot's child (a `TREE` delta pair); a selection that maps to the
already-shown view re-emits **zero** opcodes.

Semantics:
- **Properties**: `FIT_QUERY` (`0x1032`, LIST).
- **Events**: `FIT_CHANGED` (`0x13`, host → guest) — reported fit index.
- **Children**: at most one (the current selection); candidate views live
  app-side.
- **Renderer statelessness**: the measured width and derived index are layout
  output, not retained application state.

### Containers

Stacks, scroll, and other containers lay their children out inside; a Fixed box
constrains them (scroll for `SCROLLVIEW`, otherwise overflow is visible unless
`CLIPS_TO_BOUNDS` clips it).

### Size that fits (`SIZE_THAT_FITS` 0x17)

A fit slot is **size-taking on both axes**: it stretches to its parent's
proposal (`FILL` semantics — never hugs), because its **allocated width is the
unit of fitting**. It holds at most one (selected) child, laid out normally
inside the box. The renderer measures its allocated width and derives the fit
index (threshold rule in [PRIMITIVES.md](./PRIMITIVES.md#size-that-fits)). No
content-based measurement of candidates is ever done or transmitted — the query
thresholds are app-declared, so the pick is a pure function of
`(thresholds, allocated width)`.

437: /// Decode an event opcode for the **shared-memory path**, resolving
438: /// `TEXT_CHANGED` text and `NAVIGATE` URLs from the host → guest event arena
439: /// (`B` is an absolute offset into that region). Non-string events decode as
440: /// usual.
441: ///
442: /// Returns `None` for non-event opcodes, unknown commands, or string events
443: /// whose offset cannot be resolved (invalid or out of range).
444: pub fn decode_event(op: &Opcode, event_arena: &[u8]) -> Option<Event> {
445:     if op.category() != category::EVENT {
446:         return None;
447:     }
448:     if op.command() == crate::event::TEXT_CHANGED {
449:         let text = crate::arena::get_str(event_arena, op.b()).ok()?;
450:         return Some(Event::TextChanged {
451:             target: op.a(),
452:             value: text.to_string(),
453:         });
454:     }
455:     if op.command() == crate::event::NAVIGATE && op.flags() & flag::NAVIGATE_URL != 0 {
456:         let url = crate::arena::get_str(event_arena, op.b()).ok()?;
457:         return Some(Event::Navigate {
458:             url: Some(url.to_string()),
459:         });
460:     }
461:     Event::try_from(*op).ok()
462: }

The user asks: "What is the issue with gtk, that makes this so hard to implement?" — they want an explanation of why the GTK implementation of the size-that-fits fit observation is proving hard. I'm now in plan mode (read-only), so I should analyze and explain, not edit.

Let me explain clearly and concretely the obstacles I hit with the GTK renderer specifically, versus the web/DOM path. Facts:

1. **No `connect_size_allocate` signal in gtk4 0.9.7**: The exact blocker — `gtk4-0.9.7`'s `WidgetExt` (auto/widget.rs) exposes `size_allocate(&self, allocation, baseline)` — a method to *force* an allocation — but there is **no `connect_size_allocate` signal handler** in this version of gtk4-rs. In C GTK4, `size-allocate` is NOT a signal you can connect to (GTK4 removed the `size-allocate` signal that GTK3 had!). GTK3 had `GtkWidget::size-allocate` signal; GTK4 removed it. So there is **no native "my size changed" signal** to hook. That's the fundamental GTK4 constraint.

2. **GTK4 exposes size sub-classing, not observation**: In GTK4, to observe/change allocation you must **subclass `GtkWidget` and override `snapshot`/`allocate`/`measure` (GtkSizeRequest vfuncs)** — you implement a custom widget subclass with `GtkBuildable`/`GtkWidgetClass`, or use `gtk::CustomSized`/`gtk::GLArea`-style subclassing with `gtk4::subclass::prelude`. `pathland-render-gtk` currently builds **stock widgets only** (GtkBox, GtkLabel, ...) and never subclasses. Subclassing is a big architectural addition (a `GObject` subclass with class struct registration, `ObjectSubclass` derive from `glib::subclass`, size-request + allocate overrides). That's heavy and gtk4-rs-specific (glib `ObjectSubclass` boilerplate).

   Alternative observation hacks:
   - GTK4 has `GtkWidget::measure` + `gtk_widget_compute_expand` but no signal for "allocated". 
   - There is `GdkFrameClock` via `widget.add_tick_callback(...)` — a per-frame callback (vsync-driven) where you can read `widget.allocation()` / `widget.width()` and compare. This is the **pragmatic GTK4 way to observe size without subclassing**: `connect_tick` (or `add_tick_callback`) runs every frame, read `allocation().width()`. Cost: a callback per frame (60/fps) — but gated to only fit slots, and it's how many GTK apps poll size. This avoids subclassing.
   - Alternatively the deprecated-in-3-but-absent signal means: use the `tick` callback OR subclass `gtk::Widget` with `ObjectSubclass` and implement `allocate`.

3. **Renderer architecture friction**:
   - The GTK renderer is **incremental/stateless-ish**: `apply_frame` → `sync()` walks the tree, `get_or_create` builds stock widgets, `update` styles them, `sync_container` reconciles children. Widgets are rebuilt/updated every frame; there's no per-node "attach once" lifecycle seam for long-lived observers (they have `attached_sessions`, `attached_listeners` maps as idempotency guards — that's the pattern, but size observation isn't a signal they can connect).
   - The widgets map is keyed by node id and rebuilt on reconcile; attaching an observer means keying state by id + pruning on `DELETE_NODE` (doable — `fit_states` map) but the observer source (frame clock vs subclass) is the crux.
   - The fit depends on `FIT_QUERY` thresholds decoded from the arena LIST — which GTK's host decoder didn't previously handle (I added `list_csv`), and the widget needs the thresholds fresh each frame (a shared `Rc<RefCell<FitState>>`).

4. **Testing friction**: `pathland-render-gtk` tests are pure-logic (no display); a real widget allocation needs a `GtkApplication`/display. So the allocate-observation can't be unit-tested headlessly; only the pure `fit_index` (in core) and the `list_csv` parse are testable. It also means I can't easily verify the integration here.

5. **Where GTK diverges from web**: On web, the DOM has a first-class size-observation primitive — `ResizeObserver` — and CSS layout drives width; a one-liner `new ResizeObserver(cb).observe(el)`. GTK4 deliberately has **no size-change callback** (the size-allocate signal was removed in GTK4; sizes are imposed top-down by the parent). So observing sizes in GTK4 requires either subclassing (an `ObjectSubclass` with an `allocate` override) or a per-frame **tick callback** polling `allocation().width()`.

So the honest answer: the "hard part" is that **GTK4 gives you no size-change notification** — you must either (a) subclass `GtkWidget` and override `allocate`, or (b) poll on the frame clock (`add_tick_callback`), which the current stock-widget renderer has no plumbing for. The user asks: "How does GTK4 implement a similar feature by its own? Does it not have any builtin visual reactivity?"

They're asking about how GTK4 natively handles "size-based reactivity" — i.e., a widget whose visual content adapts to its allocated size. This is the key conceptual question about whether GTK4 has native mechanisms for "fit" / responsive layout / size-reactive rendering.

Let me answer accurately and professionally from knowledge of GTK4. I should not fabricate; let me ground in what GTK4 actually offers:

**GTK4's built-in mechanisms for size-reactive visuals:**

1. **`GtkStack` + `GtkStackSwitcher`** — a wizard-style container that holds multiple child pages and shows ONE, typically switched programmatically or via the switcher. Not size-reactive by default.

2. **`GtkStack` with `transition-type` and `measure`/`halign`** — not size-driven.

3. **`GtkStackSwitcher` / `GtkStackSidebar`** — selection-driven, not size-driven.

4. **`GtkConstraintLayout` (GtkGrid-style constraint solver)** — GTK4's layout constraints (`GtkConstraintLayout` with `GtkConstraintTarget`, relational constraints). This is analogous to iOS Auto Layout / CSS. You can express constraints like "width = max(320, parent*0.5)". But **constraints don't select among alternative child subtrees** — they lay out one view.

5. **`GtkBox`/grid with expand + natural-size** — responsive-ish via expand/fill/hexpand/valign; content reflows (label wraps) but no subtree switching.

6. **Native "adaptivity"**: 
   - **`GtkWindow`/responsive behavior**: GTK4's stock widgets adapt slightly (e.g., `GtkLabel` ellipsizing/wrapping, `GtkNotebook`?). 
   - **`AdwCarousel`, `AdwSplitButton`** etc. — not fit.
   - **`AdwClamp`/`AdwClampScrollable`** — clamps content to a max width (a *size constraint*, not selection). libadwaita's `AdwClamp` is close to "constrain content to a preferred width range" — measures a max-width and centers; `AdwClampScrollable` scrolls when constrained.
   - **`AdwStatusPage`** — not relevant.
   - **`AdwTabBar`/`AdwTabView`** — not relevant.
   - **`GtkStack` (again)** — and notably there IS a pattern: **`GtkStack` + `gtk_stack_set_visible_child_*`** — but selection is programmatic.

7. **The "adaptive" answer GTK wants**: In GTK4 the idiomatic approach to size-based layout switching is:
   - **`GtkConstraintLayout`** for proportional/min-max adaptive *parameter* changes (like CSS media queries on sizes, expressed as constraints).
   - **`GtkStack` + `GtkStackSwitcher`/app logic** for *mode switching* (like the tray icon ↔ menu icon): the APPLICATION decides when to switch (`gtk_stack_set_visible_child_name`) based on its own measurement — NOT automatic size-driven selection.
   - There's **no built-in "ViewThatFits" equivalent** — no container that automatically picks the first child fitting the available space. That's exactly why SwiftUI has a layout system with proposals; GTK4's model is: parent imposes size, child measures (GtkSizeRequest: measure/size_allocate), and choices like "which child" are made by the app.

8. **`GtkWidget`'s own reactivity**: GtkWidget has `measure`/`size_allocate` vfuncs (the "visual reactivity" = size request is reactive to changes: GTK4 relayouts when a widget's `queue_resize()` is called). GTK4 is **demand-driven relayout**: when a widget wants to change its natural size, it calls `queue_resize`, and GTK redoes the size negotiation. So "reactivity" to CHANGES of a widget's own size is via `queue_allocate`/`queue_resize`. But there's still no signal for "I got allocated a different size" — only the *request* side (parent re-measures), and the *draw* side (snapshot). The widget that WANTS to change its child based on the imposed size must either subclass (override allocate) or poll (tick).

9. **GtkStack's actual nearest analog**: Actually let me think harder — is there anything that picks a child by available size automatically?
   - **`GtkStack` with `hhomogeneous`/`vhomogeneous` set to FALSE** — the stack measures all children and takes the max natural size; it does NOT pick by size.
   - **`AdwViewStack`/`AdwViewSwitcher`** — selection by switcher.
   - **`GtkNotebook`** — tabs.
   - There's the old **`GtkSizeGroup`** (GTK3 deprecated) — synchronizes sizes across widgets, not selection.
   - **CSS**: GTK4 uses CSS for styling; **CSS media queries / container queries DO NOT exist in GTK CSS** (unlike web). GTK CSS has no `@media (min-width)` / container queries. So the web mechanism (pure CSS `@container` bands, which was the earlier design for SizeThatFits) **has no GTK CSS analog**.

So the honest answer:
- GTK4 has **no built-in ViewThatFits/SizeThatFits** — no container that auto-picks a child based on its allocation.
- Its "visual reactivity" model is: (a) **size negotiation** (GtkSizeRequest — widgets propose/measure, parents allocate; changes propagate via `queue_resize` rather than signals), (b) **constraint-based adaptive layout** (`GtkConstraintLayout` for min/max/proportional parameters — the closest thing to CSS media queries on size), (c) **app-driven mode selection** (`GtkStack` pages switched by the app, AdwViewStack/ViewSwitcher for user-driven switching), and (d) **shadow: `AdwClamp`** for max-width clamping (a constraint, not selection).
- So a Pathland `SizeThatFits` is genuinely ADDITIVE to GTK — the renderer must implement the observation itself (tick or subclass), which is exactly why we hit the friction. On web, the browser ships `ResizeObserver` + CSS `@container` (native size-observability); GTK4 deliberately does not provide that primitive, because its design puts that decision in the application (via GtkStack/constraints) rather than in a "responsive container".

Also worth noting the "measure"/`GtkSizeRequest` angle for a DIFFERENT implementation: you could implement fit-observation via `measure()` overrides, but measurement is the request side — the widget asks "what natural sizes?"; allocation is imposed. GTK4 separates measure (what you want) from allocate (what you get) with no callback between. Web's ResizeObserver corresponds to neither — it's purely "your box changed".

Let me also mention: `GtkStack` — if the app knows the breakpoint, GTK's answer here would be `GtkStack` + the app switching on its own measurement — which maps EXACTLY to our original "app-side selection" design. But Pathland chose "renderer does measurement locally, reports only transitions, transmits only the selected child" — which is in-between, and GTK has no native container for that; hence the implementation is on us.

## The three built-in reactivity models in GTK4

**1. Size negotiation / demand-driven relayout** (`gtk4-0.9.7/src/auto/widget.rs`): a widget declares its natural sizes via the `GtkSizeRequest` vfuncs (`measure`/`size_allocate`); to *request* a relayout it calls `queue_resize()`/`queue_allocate()` and GTK re-runs the negotiation. So "I changed what I want" is reactive — but the *imposed* size flows **down from the parent**, and there is **no callback/signal when a widget's allocation changes** (the GTK3 `size-allocate` signal was removed; that's the exact blocker we hit). A widget only learns its size by overriding `allocate` (subclass) or sampling it (tick callback).

**2. Constraint-based adaptive layout** — `GtkConstraintLayout` (`constraint_layout.rs`): Auto-Layout-style relational/target constraints (`width ≥ 320`, `width = parent·0.5`, preferred-range). This is GTK's "responsive *parameters*" primitive — the analog of CSS media queries on size — but it adapts *one* view's geometry; it never selects among **alternative subtrees**.

**3. App-/user-driven page switching** — `GtkStack` + `gtk_stack_set_visible_child_name`, and libadwaita's `AdwViewStack`/`AdwViewSwitcher` (`view_stack.rs`): show one child out of many, but selection is **programmatic (the app) or user-driven (a switcher)** — never automatic by available width.

Plus the "readability" extras: **`AdwClamp`/`AdwClampScrollable`** (`clamp.rs`) constrain content to a preferred max-width (a sizing constraint, not a switch), and labels wrap/ellipsize. All of these are *parameter* adaptivity; GTK CSS has **no `@container`/media queries** (confirmed — nothing in the CSS parser), so the pure-CSS web approach we rejected earlier has literally no GTK analog.

## Why this matters for our design

GTK's own idiomatic answer to "narrow layout vs. wide layout" is **`GtkStack` + the app deciding** — i.e., exactly the app-side selection model. But you deliberately chose the other model: *only the selected child is transmitted + the renderer measures and derives the fit locally*. That model is **genuinely additive to GTK** — it requires the renderer to observe its own allocation, a capability GTK4 withholds (no signal, no CSS container queries, no auto-fit container). On the web the browser hands us `ResizeObserver` + CSS `@container` for free; on GTK we must build the observation ourselves — which is precisely the ~40-line tick-callback (or subclass `allocate`) seam we discussed.

So: no, it's not that GTK4 is missing "visual reactivity" — it's that its reactivity is parent-imposed, constraint-based, and app-selected, and our chosen semantics live outside all three.

## SwiftUI — **has the feature natively**
`ViewThatFits` is a first-party layout container (iOS 16+/macOS 13+). Because SwiftUI **owns measurement**: a view answers `sizeThatFits(_ proposal:)` with its ideal size, and the layout engine proposes sizes and picks the first child that fits — no signal, no polling, no window. `GeometryReader` additionally hands a view its own size for custom adaptive layouts. "Only the pick renders" is inherent (it's a layout decision).

## Jetpack Compose — **has the feature natively**
Same story: `androidx.compose.foundation.layout.ViewThatFits` (Compose 1.5+) is a `Layout` that measures children against the incoming `Constraints` and keeps the first that fits; `BoxWithConstraints` exposes the parent constraints (`maxWidth`) for hand-written breakpoints. Measurement is engine-owned, so the pick is just a measurement pass, and size changes re-run composition/layout — no observer plumbing needed.

## Qt — **observability is easy; no auto-fit primitive**
two flavors:
- **QtWidgets**: unlike GTK4, it kept a per-widget resize notification — **`QWidget::resizeEvent(QResizeEvent*)`** is a real native callback (GTK4's missing primitive exists here). Switching between layouts is app-driven (`QStackedLayout`/`QStackedWidget`), like GTK, but observing your own size is trivial.
- **Qt QML**: size *is* a reactive property — `width`/`height` are bindable, so "react to my own width" is idiomatic (`width >= 640 ? wide : narrow`, `onWidthChanged`). There's no named `ViewThatFits`, but the pattern is a few binding lines rather than framework machinery.

## GTK4 — **the genuine outlier**
No size-change signal, no measurement-owned "pick" primitive, no `@container`/media-query CSS. Its reactivity is parent-imposed + constraint-based + app-selected — so both the *observation* (tick/subclass) **and** the *selection* (the app) are on you.

## The underlying reason

| Toolkit | Owns measurement? | Auto-fit primitive | Own-size observation |
|---|---|---|---|
| SwiftUI | yes (layout engine) | `ViewThatFits` ✓ | engine proposals |
| Compose | yes (measure pass) | `ViewThatFits` ✓ | `Constraints`/`BoxWithConstraints` |
| Qt QML | reactive props | none (but trivial via bindings) | `width` bindable ✓ |
| QtWidgets | no | none | `resizeEvent()` ✓ |
| GTK4 | no | none | ✗ (removed signal; tick/subclass) |

Frameworks that **own measurement and layout** (SwiftUI, Compose) can offer automatic fit natively, because "which child fits" is a layout decision *inside* their engine. The widget-toolkit family (GTK4, QtWidgets) hands layout to negotiation instead, so auto-fit is outside the toolkit — and GTK4 additionally stripped the size notification, making it the only one where even *observing* the size is extra work.
